units.title: General Geography - Earth in the Solar System, Motions, Time, Seasons, Interior of the Earth, Landforms, Atmosphere, Climate, Oceans, Hydrological Disasters, Marine and Continental Resources

rows.title: The universe and the solar system - origin theories, the Sun, planets, asteroids, comets, meteors
sub: Group-II S2-1: The Earth in our solar system - the Sun, planets and the origin of the earth

secs.t: Planets - order, inner vs outer, superlatives, planets without satellites, satellite counts

x: Exam angle: "no natural satellite", "retrograde rotation" and "least dense" are the most repeated one-liners.
The asteroid belt lies between the orbits of
Mars and Jupiter
and separates the inner and outer planets.
The four inner planets are rocky or terrestrial, while the outer planets comprise two gas giants and two ice giants.
Jupiter is the most massive planet and has approximately
318 times
the mass of Earth.
Venus and Uranus
rotate in the retrograde direction, from east to west.
Mercury
remains closest to Earth for the longest time on average because its small orbit keeps it relatively near the other planets.
The new moons were announced by the International Astronomical Union through its Minor Planet Centre, which verified the discoveries.
Pluto orbits the Sun and is nearly round, but
it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood
The recognised dwarf planets listed are
Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake and Eris
Uranus has a highly tilted axis and rotates nearly on its side.
Mercury
has the largest day-night temperature gap, exceeding 1000°F, because of its slow rotation and very thin atmosphere.

secs.t: Origin theories → proponent; age of the universe, most abundant element

x: Kant proposed the Nebular hypothesis in 1755, Laplace revised it in 1796, and Chamberlin and Moulton proposed the Planetesimal hypothesis in 1904.
The Nebular hypothesis dates to 1755, the Planetesimal hypothesis to 1904, the Big Bang theory to 1927, and the Steady State theory to 1948.
The
red-shift
of receding galaxies, observed in the context of Hubble's work in 1929, is evidence for the expansion of the universe.
Cosmic Microwave Background radiation
is regarded as the leftover glow of the Big Bang and supports the theory.
Rocky planets formed mainly in the hot inner disc, while the cool outer disc retained volatile ices associated with giant planets.

secs.t: Sun - layers, surface temperature, size, sunspots, solar flares

x: The
core
is the region where hydrogen nuclei undergo nuclear fusion to form helium, at a temperature of approximately 15 million °C.
The photosphere is the visible surface, the chromosphere appears reddish, and the corona is the very hot outer atmosphere.
The photosphere has a temperature of approximately 5,500–6,000°C, while the corona can exceed one million °C. Thus, the corona is hotter than the visible surface despite being farther out.
The sunspot cycle is matched by plasma currents in the approximately 35,000-km-deep
Near-Surface Shear Layer
Solar flares and coronal mass ejections can cause geomagnetic storms and auroras and can disrupt or damage satellites, communication, navigation and power-grid systems.

secs.t: Cosmology terms and distance units

x: The Goldilocks zone, or habitable zone, is the region around a star where conditions may permit liquid water because temperatures are neither too high nor too low.
The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy with a rotating disc, central bulge and a halo containing dark matter.
Indian researchers identified the spiral galaxy Alaknanda using the
James Webb Space Telescope
(JWST).

secs.t: Moons and planetary features

x: Ganymede is larger than Mercury, Europa has a subsurface ocean beneath ice, and Charon is Pluto's largest moon.
Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium, while methane gives Uranus and Neptune their blue-green tints.
The re-analysis suggests that Titan probably lacks a global subsurface ocean and instead has a partly molten ice-water mixture with local warm-water pockets, reaching up to about 20°C.

secs.t: Stars and space objects - life cycle, nebulae, Cepheids, pulsars, neutron stars, black holes

x: A massive star evolves into a supergiant, undergoes a supernova explosion, and may end as a neutron star or black hole.
Polaris is in Ursa Minor, lies close to the north celestial pole, and stars twinkle more noticeably than planets.
Because of the wobble of Earth's axis,
Vega
is expected to become the pole star in about 12,000 years.

secs.t: Asteroids, comets, meteors, meteorites; asteroid missions

x: The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of
Mars and Jupiter
and consists largely of rocky remnants of the early Solar System.
Solar heating develops the tail near the Sun, and solar radiation and wind cause it to point away from the Sun; comets originate from the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud.
A meteor is the streak of light produced when a meteoroid burns in the atmosphere; the surviving fragment that reaches the ground is a
meteorite
OSIRIS-REx returned Bennu samples, DART impacted Dimorphos, Hera surveys the Didymos-Dimorphos system, and Hayabusa2 obtained samples from Ryugu.

secs.t: Dwarf planets and planet-status changes

x: Pluto satisfies the orbiting and nearly round conditions but has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood, so it was classified as a dwarf planet.
All three statements are correct: Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930; it is the largest known Kuiper Belt object and lies at approximately 39 AU.
The discovery of
Eris
, along with the need for a clearer planetary definition, helped prompt Pluto's reclassification as a dwarf planet in 2006.

secs.t: Indian solar and planetary missions and Lagrange points

x: Aditya-L1 completed one year at L1 on 6 January 2025, while the halo orbit provides continuous solar observation, low fuel use and an expected five-year life.
Mangalyaan is the Mars orbiter, Aditya-L1 is the solar observatory, Aryabhata was the first Indian satellite, and SMILE studies the solar wind-magnetic shield interaction.

secs.t: Earth's unique features - Goldilocks zone, Earth-like planets, evolution of the spheres

x: K2-18b is approximately 124 light-years away in Leo, about 5.2 times wider and around nine times more massive than Earth; a possible biomarker molecule has been reported for it.
The early hydrogen-helium atmosphere was lost to the solar wind; interior degassing followed, producing water vapour, nitrogen and carbon dioxide, and photosynthesis later added oxygen.
The geodynamo generated by churning liquid iron in the outer core produces Earth's magnetic field, which shields the planet from the solar wind.

secs.t: Orbit terms - perihelion, aphelion, perigee, apogee

x: Perigee is the Moon's nearest approach to Earth; a full Moon at perigee is called a
supermoon
and produces higher tides.
Seasons result primarily from
the tilt of Earth's axis
, not from Earth-Sun distance; northern winter coincides with perihelion.
The Earth reaches perihelion, its nearest point to the Sun, around 3 January, at a distance of approximately 147 million kilometres.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Aditya-L1 data helped decode how the October 2024 solar storm compressed Earth's magnetic field.
Aditya-L1's VELC payload made
the first visible-light spectroscopic observations of coronal mass ejections
, or CMEs.
SMILE will image the solar wind interaction with Earth's magnetic shield using X-ray and ultraviolet observations together.
Sriharikota's SDSC-SHAR launched Aditya-L1 on PSLV-C57 in 2023 and completed its 100th launch on 29 January 2025.

rows.title: Earth - shape, size, geoid; latitudes and longitudes, the graticule

secs.t: Parallels and meridians → countries they pass through

x: The Prime Meridian passes through the United Kingdom, France, Spain, Algeria, Mali, Burkina Faso, Togo and Ghana.
The Equator crosses Gabon, Uganda and Somalia, but it does not touch
India
The Tropic of Capricorn at 23°26' S crosses
Chile, Argentina, Paraguay and Brazil
The Arctic Circle lies at approximately 66°33' N and the Antarctic Circle at approximately 66°33' S. They mark the approximate limits of polar day and polar night.

secs.t: Relative position of cities (world and Indian)

x: The correct north-to-south order is Srinagar, Bhopal, Visakhapatnam and Chennai.
Delhi is at about 28.6°N, Visakhapatnam at 17.7°N, Hyderabad at 17.4°N and Thiruvananthapuram at about 8°N. Hence the order is 2, 4, 1, 3.
Kibithu in Arunachal Pradesh is the most eastward location, while Guhar Moti in Gujarat is the most westward location.

secs.t: Dimensions - diameters, circumference, land-water ratio

x: The equatorial diameter is about 12,756 km, the polar diameter about 12,714 km, their difference is about 43 km, and the mean radius is approximately 6,371 km.
The surface area of the Earth is approximately
510 million square kilometres
Approximately 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by water and 29% is land.

secs.t: Graticule - parallels at 1°, great vs small circles, valid coordinates, 0°-0° point

x: The
Equator
is the only parallel whose plane passes through the centre of the Earth and is therefore a great circle.
Latitude ranges from 0° to 90° north or south and longitude from 0° to 180° east or west.
The intersection of the Equator and the Prime Meridian, represented by 0° latitude and 0° longitude, lies in the
Gulf of Guinea in the Atlantic Ocean

secs.t: Shape of the earth - geoid, oblate spheroid, evidences, nearest point to centre

x: The polar radius is shortest; therefore, the surface point nearest the Earth's centre is near the poles, specifically
the Arctic Ocean floor near the North Pole
Melting ice redistributes mass towards the Equator, enhances the equatorial bulge, slows rotation and lengthens the day by about 1.33 milliseconds per century.
The
Survey of India
is building a Geoid Model for the whole country to support precise GPS/GNSS-based height determination.

secs.t: Longitudes - Prime Meridian, degree-to-distance relation

x: The distance represented by one degree of longitude decreases towards the poles because meridians converge: it is about 111 km at the Equator, 55.5 km at 60° and zero at the poles.
The Mercator projection enlarges polar areas and results in the relative shrinking of Africa.
The
African Union
backed the ‘Correct the Map’ campaign, which highlighted distortions associated with the Mercator projection.

secs.t: Latitude-longitude extent of India and AP mainland (extreme points)

x: Mainland India extends from 8°4′N to 37°6′N and from 68°7′E to 97°25′E. The other ranges refer to Andhra Pradesh, an overall southern extreme or an incorrect older figure.
India has an area of approximately 32,87,263 square kilometres, ranks seventh in area, and measures about 3,214 km north-south and 2,933 km east-west.
All four directional relationships are correct: Chhattisgarh and Odisha lie to the north, Telangana to the west and north-west, Karnataka to the south-west, and Tamil Nadu to the south.

secs.t: Antipodes and position-finding on the grid

x: To find the antipode, change north to south and subtract the longitude from 180°.
The antipode of x°N, y°E is
. Antipodes are diametrically opposite points on the Earth's surface.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The UN resolution dated 8 September 2026 was associated with the
Equal Earth map
EOS-05 is described as India's first Earth-imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit, at approximately 36,000 km, allowing frequent observation of the same area.
Andhra Pradesh lies wholly between the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer and is described as having a tropical Aw climate.

rows.title: Motions of the earth - rotation and revolution; effects (day and night, Coriolis force, tides)

secs.t: Rotation - direction, period, speed with latitude, circle of illumination, why not felt

x: As the Earth rotates, a place generally passes through two tidal bulges, producing two high tides and two low tides, with successive similar tides about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.
Redistribution of mass towards the Equator increases moment of inertia and slightly slows Earth's rotation, lengthening the day by about 1.33 milliseconds per century.
At the
equinoxes
, the circle of illumination passes through both poles and day and night are nearly equal across the Earth.

secs.t: Coriolis force - deflection, variation with latitude and wind speed, Ferrel's law

x: Ferrel's law states that the Coriolis effect deflects moving air and water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Coriolis force is very weak near the Equator, so it generally cannot provide sufficient rotational deflection for cyclone formation within about 5° latitude.

secs.t: Revolution - orbit shape, perihelion, aphelion, speed, period

x: The Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical, with the Sun located at one of the two foci of the ellipse.
The Sun's gravitational attraction acts as the centripetal force that keeps the Earth revolving around it.
The changing Earth-Sun distance between perihelion and aphelion slightly affects tidal ranges.

secs.t: Day and night - causes, day-length variation, midnight sun

x: The statement that all places experience equal day and night throughout the year is incorrect.
The
midnight sun
refers to continuous daylight for 24 hours or more in high-latitude regions during their summer.
Because of the Earth's axial inclination and revolution, the poles experience approximately six months of daylight followed by approximately six months of night.

secs.t: Sidereal vs solar day, leap year

x: A sidereal day, measured relative to a distant star, lasts 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds.
The accumulated extra quarter day produces a leap year with 29 February approximately every four years, with exceptions for century years.
A century year is a leap year only when divisible by 400.

secs.t: Evidences and experiments of rotation (Foucault pendulum)

x: In Foucault's 1851 experiment at Paris, the plane of swing of the pendulum slowly turned, providing visible evidence of Earth's rotation.
The constant Earth-Sun distance is not an evidence of Earth's rotation; in fact, the distance varies slightly because Earth's orbit is elliptical.

secs.t: Twilight duration variation with latitude

x: Twilight is the period of
diffused light before sunrise and after sunset
, when the Sun is below or near the horizon.
Twilight is shortest at the Equator because the Sun rises and sets nearly vertically.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Cyclone movement is influenced by steering winds and broader atmospheric circulation, while the Coriolis effect influences its deflection and rotation.

rows.title: Concept of time - local and standard time, GMT/UTC, Indian Standard Time, time zones, International Date Line
sub: Group-II S2-2: Motions of the earth, latitudes and longitudes, local and standard time, IDL

secs.t: Local time calculation from longitude difference

x: The Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, giving
of longitude for every hour of time.
Since one degree of longitude equals four minutes of time, one minute of arc equals four seconds of time.
Thirty degrees correspond to two hours, and a place west of Greenwich is behind Greenwich Mean Time.
The longitudinal span is approximately 29°, which corresponds to about 116 minutes, or nearly two hours.
The journey takes three hours and the eastward movement adds one hour because 15° equals one hour.

secs.t: Indian Standard Time - meridian, reference town, states crossed, IST-GMT offset, two-time-zone debate

x: The intersection of the 82°30'E meridian and the Tropic of Cancer occurs in
Chhattisgarh
Indian Standard Time is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT/UTC, so 0000 UTC corresponds to
Separate Bombay and Calcutta times date from 1884, a single IST was adopted after 1947, the White Rabbit network was inaugurated in July 2026, and the Rules were notified on 27 August 2026.
The Rules make IST the single mandatory reference for
legal, administrative, commercial and official purposes
The network provides sub-nanosecond synchronisation over fibre and is designed to reduce dependence on GPS.
NavIC times its signals using
rubidium atomic clocks
The north-east experiences sunrise considerably earlier than western India, creating the basis for the separate-time-zone debate.
The debate has included advancing IST by 30 minutes, creating a north-eastern zone about one hour ahead, and retaining 82°30'E as the reference for the national time system.
A 30-degree longitudinal span corresponds to about two hours of local-time difference between Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat.

secs.t: International Date Line - ocean, strait, crossing rule, deviations, neighbours

x: Crossing the International Date Line eastward causes the calendar date to go back by one day; consequently, one day is repeated.
Big Diomede belongs to Russia and Little Diomede belongs to the United States; they lie close to each other in the Bering Strait but on different calendar dates.
Samoa shifted to the Asian side of the International Date Line in 2011, thereby changing its calendar relationship with nearby countries.

secs.t: Time zones - number, countries with most zones, cities sharing clock time

x: The theoretical system divides 360° of longitude into 24 time zones, each 15° wide.
France
has 12 time zones when its overseas territories are included, while Russia has 11.
China
uses one official time zone throughout the country despite its large longitudinal span.
Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and
Colombo
observe UTC+5:30.
Nepal observes
, whereas Indian Standard Time is UTC+5:30, creating a 15-minute difference.

secs.t: Local time gap across India (Arunachal vs Gujarat)

x: The nearly two-hour difference in sunrise is primarily due to the large east-west longitudinal extent between Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat.

secs.t: GMT/UTC - Greenwich, atomic basis, natural vs conventional units

x: GMT denotes mean solar time at Greenwich.
A day, month and year are natural time units linked respectively with Earth’s rotation, the Moon’s revolution and Earth’s revolution.

secs.t: Daylight saving time concept

x: In many mid- and high-latitude countries, clocks are advanced by about one hour during summer to extend evening daylight and are set back in autumn.
Daylight Saving Time is intended to make better use of available evening daylight in summer.

secs.t: Tropic of Cancer - Indian states, nearby cities, meeting point with the standard meridian

x: Exam angle: "how many states" (8), "which state is NOT crossed" (Odisha, UP and Bihar are common distractors).
The Tropic of Cancer lies at approximately 23°26′N, commonly rounded to 23.5°N.
Andhra Pradesh lies wholly south of the Tropic of Cancer
Agartala
is one of the Indian cities situated on or near the Tropic of Cancer.

secs.t: Revolution effects - solstices, equinoxes, seasons, day length

x: Exam angle: APPSC matched winter solstice with 22 Dec, summer with 21 Jun, vernal with 21 Mar, autumnal with Sep 23. It has also accepted "20 or 21 March" and "22 or 23 September" as equinox dates.
The Northern Hemisphere experiences its winter solstice on
22 December
, when the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn.
Seasons result mainly from the tilt of Earth’s axis combined with Earth’s revolution around the Sun, which changes the angle and duration of solar illumination.
During southern summer, the
South Pole
is tilted towards the Sun, producing longer days and summer conditions in the Southern Hemisphere.

secs.t: Axial tilt and inclination - consequences, observed shift

x: The Earth's axis makes an angle of
with the plane of its orbit, equivalent to a tilt of 23½° from the perpendicular.
Axial tilt is responsible for seasons and unequal day length, and it determines the positions of both the tropics and polar circles.
Long-period variations in Earth's orbit and axial behaviour that influence climate are called
Milankovitch cycles

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The White Rabbit IST network enables synchronised IST time-stamps for banking, digital payments, railways, airports, power grids and telecom, and helps protect against GPS spoofing.
The wide east-west extent creates a daylight disadvantage in the north-east.
The 82.5°E meridian used for Indian Standard Time passes through
Kakinada district
in Andhra Pradesh.

rows.title: Seasons - inclination of the axis, solstices and equinoxes, distribution of insolation

secs.t: Causes of seasons and day-length variation

x: Seasonal variation results from the Earth’s axial inclination, the parallelism of its axis, its revolution around the Sun and its spherical shape.
A hemisphere tilted towards the Sun receives more direct insolation and longer daylight, producing summer conditions.
The Earth’s axis maintains its parallelism during revolution and generally points towards the Pole Star.

secs.t: Seasonal contrast by latitude zone

x: Seasonal differences are greatest in
high latitudes
because the annual swings in day length and insolation are very large there.
Low latitudes commonly have wet and dry seasons, subtropical regions have hot summers and mild winters, and mid-latitudes show four distinct seasons.

secs.t: Seasons in northern vs southern hemisphere

x: The Northern Hemisphere has its longest day around 21 June, while the Southern Hemisphere has its longest day around 22 December.
Australia lies in the Southern Hemisphere, where December corresponds to
summer

secs.t: Noon shadow length and June day length at Indian cities

x: Only places between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn can receive the overhead Sun.
On 21 June, the Sun is overhead at
the Tropic of Cancer
, so an object there casts no shadow at local noon.
Andhra Pradesh extends approximately from 12°41′N to 19°07′N, between the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer.

secs.t: Insolation distribution - angle, day length, latitude

x: The major factors listed are the angle of incidence, duration of day, atmospheric transparency and land configuration.
Vertical rays are more concentrated over a smaller area and usually pass through a shorter atmospheric path, producing stronger heating than oblique rays.
A temperature of approximately 50°C was recorded at
Ganganagar in 1935
during India’s hot weather conditions.

secs.t: Perihelion/aphelion vs seasons misconception

x: The Earth reaches aphelion, its greatest distance from the Sun, around
4 July
, during Northern Hemisphere summer.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Andhra Pradesh experiences summer from March to May, the South-West monsoon from June to September, and winter from October to February.
The IMD identifies four seasons: winter, pre-monsoon, South-West monsoon and post-monsoon.
The traditional Indian calendar recognises six ritus, beginning with Vasanta and extending to Shishira.
The theme associated with the International Day of Yoga in 2026 is “
Yoga for Healthy Ageing

rows.title: Interior of the earth - crust, mantle, core; discontinuities and seismic evidence
sub: Group-II S2-3: Interior of the earth - crust, mantle, core and the discontinuities

secs.t: Discontinuities → between which layers

x: The
Conrad Discontinuity
lies within the crust and separates the upper crust from the lower crust, broadly corresponding to SIAL and SIMA.
The Repetti Discontinuity lies within the mantle and separates its upper and lower portions at roughly 700–1,000 km depth.
The Moho separates crust and mantle, varies in depth beneath continents and oceans, and was identified by Andrija Mohorovicic in 1909.

secs.t: Sources of information - direct vs indirect

x: Exam angle: APPSC G1 2017 - "surface rock from mining areas" is the only direct source among seismic, gravity and magnetic options.
Seismic waves
are an indirect source because their behaviour reveals the structure and properties of inaccessible interior layers.
Meteorites and gravity anomalies are indirect sources, while magma and lava brought out by volcanic eruptions are direct evidence.

secs.t: Composition of layers - SIAL, SIMA, NIFE; constituents of the core

x: SIMA consists chiefly of silica and magnesium, is basaltic in character and is regarded as a source of magma.
NIFE represents nickel and iron, is associated with the core, has a density of approximately 11 and helps explain Earth's magnetism.
Oxygen is the most abundant element by weight in the crust, followed by
silicon
at approximately 27.72%.
The crustal percentages are oxygen 46.60%, silicon 27.72%, aluminium 8.13% and iron 5.00%.

secs.t: Seismic waves through layers - P and S behaviour, shadow zone

x: Since S-waves cannot travel through
liquid
s and vanish on reaching the outer core, the outer core is inferred to be liquid.
Changes in density alter seismic-wave velocity and produce reflection and refraction at boundaries, revealing internal discontinuities.
The P-wave shadow zone is the belt approximately 105°–145° from the epicentre where direct P-waves are not recorded.

secs.t: Earth's magnetic field - origin, axis inclination

x: The Earth's magnetic axis is inclined approximately
to its geographic axis.
Both statements are true, and convection of molten iron producing dynamo action directly explains why the outer core generates Earth's magnetic field.

secs.t: Layers - crust, mantle, core: thickness, density, state

x: Oceanic crust is approximately 5 km thick, whereas continental crust is approximately 30 km thick, though it may reach greater thickness beneath mountains.
The mantle extends downward from the Moho to approximately
depth.
The IUGG division identifies mantle zones at Moho–200 km, 200–700 km and 700–2,900 km.
Continental crust is associated with granitic SIAL, whereas oceanic crust is associated with basaltic SIMA.

secs.t: Asthenosphere and lithosphere - location and role

x: The asthenosphere is a weak, plastic and partly molten upper-mantle zone, generally associated with depths of 100–200 km, and is a major source of magma.
The dense lower layer of the Indian plate is reported to be peeling away and delaminating into the mantle at roughly 100 km depth beneath Tibet.

secs.t: Temperature, pressure, density gradient with depth

x: Temperature rises by approximately 1°C for every 32 m of depth in the upper crust, although the rate slows at greater depths.
Density increases downward from approximately 2.8–3.0 g/cm³ in the crust to 4.6 in the mantle and 13.3–13.6 in the inner core.
The immense pressure caused by the weight of overlying material keeps the inner core solid despite its extreme temperature.

secs.t: Core - outer vs inner core, constituents besides iron and nickel

x: Exam angle: "Nickel and Ferrum" as the core's main elements; "Silicon" as the extra constituent.
The churning motion of molten iron in the liquid outer core drives the geodynamo, which generates Earth's magnetic field.
Swarm satellite observations indicated a shift beneath the Pacific from sluggish westward flow to strong eastward flow, followed by weakening around 2020.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The global mapping referred to mantle earthquakes occurring more than 80 km below the Moho; their surface shaking is generally weak.
Diamonds formed in the mantle are transported upward to the crust through
kimberlite pipes
The magnetic field generated by the liquid outer core helps shield life from the solar wind and cosmic radiation.

rows.title: Rocks and minerals - igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic; the rock cycle
sub: Group-II S2-4: Rocks - igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic; the rock cycle

secs.t: Crustal elements by abundance - most/least abundant, second-most abundant metal

x: Exam angle: "most abundant metal" = aluminium, not iron; "most abundant element" = oxygen; whole-Earth question = iron.
Silicon ranks second at about 27.7%, iron is the second-most abundant metal at about 5.0%, and magnesium ranks eighth among the listed eight elements at about 1.5%.
SIAL has a density of about 2.9, SIMA is basaltic and associated with magma, and NIFE forms the nickel-iron core with a density of about 11.

secs.t: Rock types → examples and odd-one-out; petrology

x: Petrology
is the branch of geology concerned with the study of rocks.
Sandstone, limestone, shale and conglomerate
are sedimentary rocks.
Marble, slate and quartzite are metamorphic rocks, whereas
limestone
is a sedimentary rock and a parent rock of marble.

secs.t: Igneous - intrusive vs extrusive, felsic vs mafic

x: Exam angle: A-R item - "felsic rocks are high in Fe, Mg, Ca" is FALSE; that describes mafic rocks.
Granite is felsic intrusive, rhyolite is felsic extrusive, diorite is intermediate intrusive and basalt is mafic extrusive.
Andesite, dacite, rhyolite and basalt are volcanic rocks, and they generally require more energy to fracture than many sedimentary rocks.

secs.t: Rock-forming minerals and silicate classes; Bowen's series; Mohs scale

x: Muscovite is a phyllosilicate, albite is a tectosilicate, hornblende is a double-chain inosilicate and augite is a single-chain inosilicate.
The discontinuous branch proceeds from olivine to pyroxene, amphibole and biotite as magma cools.
Quartz is silicon dioxide (SiO2), is relatively hard and resistant to weathering, and is a major component of granite and sandstone.

secs.t: Fossils and fossil fuels by rock type

x: Sedimentary rocks
commonly preserve fossils and host coal, petroleum and natural gas.
Sandstone and other sedimentary rocks may preserve fossils and contain fossil fuels.
Dravidian or Palaeozoic rocks contain abundant marine fossils, while Archaean rocks formed before life and generally contain none.
Mount Everest is described as being composed of
Upper Carboniferous limestone

secs.t: Metamorphic - parent → metamorphosed rock; typical minerals

x: Clay or shale metamorphoses into
slate
; with further metamorphism, slate may develop into schist.
Coal may pass through anthracite during metamorphism and ultimately form
graphite
Metamorphism involves recrystallisation under heat and pressure, without complete melting of the rock.
Thermal or contact metamorphism and regional or dynamic metamorphism are the broad forms identified in this classification.
Marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss and schist
are metamorphic rocks.

secs.t: Sedimentary rocks - formation, stratification, porosity vs permeability

x: Sediments are transported, deposited, compacted and cemented into successive layers called strata.
Clay contains pore spaces but its very fine particles prevent the easy passage of water; hence it is
porous but impermeable
Chalk and sandstone are porous and permeable, clay is porous but impermeable, whereas
granite
is generally neither porous nor permeable.

secs.t: Rock cycle - processes linking the three types

x: Surface rocks undergo weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition; lithification forms sedimentary rocks, heat and pressure form metamorphic rocks, and melting produces magma.
Melting converts metamorphic rock into
magma
, which may later cool to form igneous rock.
Mantle material reaching the surface as magma or lava cools and forms
igneous rocks

secs.t: Rock systems of India - composition and what each holds

x: The Dharwar system contains high-grade
iron ore, manganese, copper, lead and gold
and is economically the most important system.
The Tertiary system spans approximately the Eocene to Pliocene, includes Himalayan sediments, Karewas, Bhangar and Khadar, and is associated with petroleum.
Archaean and Dharwar are the oldest groups, followed by the Purana Cuddapah, Gondwana, Deccan Trap and Tertiary systems in the stated broad sequence.

secs.t: Rock study terms - petrology, lithology, geological time scale

x: Petrology
is the branch of geology concerned with the study of rocks.
Lithology describes the physical character of a rock unit, particularly its texture, grain size and composition.
Giovanni Arduino developed the geological time scale in 1760, the Standard time scale was set in Italy in 1881, and the Indian time scale was advocated by Sir T.H. Holland.

secs.t: Rocks of AP - Cuddapah basin, Khondalites, Charnockites, Deccan trap → region

x: Gondwana is associated with coal, Deccan Trap patches consist of basalt linked with black cotton soil, the KG basin has marine sediments, and the Cuddapah basin is Proterozoic sedimentary.

The Eastern Ghats mobile belt contains bauxite, manganese and graphite; Gondwana contains coal; coastal sands contain ilmenite, rutile and zircon; and the Kurnool Group contains cement-grade limestone.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The study reported that glacier-crushed pyrite in the upper Indus basin releases carbon dioxide
about three times faster
than silicate weathering removes it.

All three statements are correct: Kadapa-Kurnool limestone supports the cement industry, Eastern Ghats mining requires social and ecological safeguards, and gold mining is reviving at Ramagiri in the Dharwar greenstone belt.

rows.title: Earth movements - continental drift, sea-floor spreading, plate tectonics and plate boundaries
sub: Group-II S2-5: Plate tectonics, continental drift, folding and faulting

secs.t: Continental drift - proponent, supercontinent, ocean, evidences

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2025 counted rock belts, placer gold and a third evidence as ALL correct.
The jigsaw fit of South America and Africa is best demonstrated along the
continental-shelf edges
Bullard's 1964 computer analysis demonstrated the close fit between the continental margins of South America and Africa.
The Ghana coast has placer gold but lacks the corresponding source rock; the source is located in the Brazil plateau, suggesting former continental continuity.

secs.t: Gondwanaland vs Laurasia - present landmasses; India's parent landmass

x: The Peninsular Plateau was part of the
African landmass
until the Cretaceous period.

The breakup of Gondwanaland occurred about 225 million years ago, the Peninsular Plateau separated from Africa during the Cretaceous, Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, and the Himalayas rose about 65 million years ago.
After the breakup of Gondwanaland, the Indian craton moved northwards towards the
Eurasian craton

secs.t: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

x: The Cocos Plate subducts beneath the Caribbean Plate, and this setting is associated with
Volcan de Fuego
Divergent boundaries involve plates moving apart and the formation of new crust; the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is an example.
Convergent boundaries involve collision or subduction and may produce
trenches, island arcs and the Andes
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is divergent, the Himalaya is continent–continent convergent, the Andes is ocean–continent convergent, and the San Andreas Fault is transform.

secs.t: Sea-floor spreading - proponent, palaeomagnetism, crust age and thickness

x: Harry Hess
proposed the sea-floor spreading hypothesis in the early 1960s, including the creation of new crust at mid-ocean ridges and its destruction at trenches.
At mid-ocean ridges, rising magma forms new oceanic crust and pushes the existing crust sideways; older crust is eventually destroyed at trenches.
Vine and Matthews
explained the symmetrical magnetic stripes as evidence supporting sea-floor spreading in 1963.

secs.t: Plate boundaries - example → type

x: The Red Sea and East African Rift are divergent settings associated with the separation of the Nubian, Somalian and Arabian plates near the Afar triple junction.
Earthquakes occur at all three major boundary types: through stretching at divergent boundaries, subduction-related friction at convergent boundaries, and sudden slip at transform boundaries.

secs.t: Indian plate - drift direction, rate, collision history

x: The Deccan Traps erupted as the northward-moving Indian Plate crossed near the equator and passed over the Reunion hotspot.
Delamination refers to the denser lower layer of the plate peeling away and sinking into the mantle at approximately 100 kilometres depth.
The Ladakh Magmatic Arc formed through
northward subduction of the Neo-Tethys Plate
and lies between the Indus and Shyok suture zones.

secs.t: Convection current theory - proponent and mechanism

x: Arthur Holmes
proposed the convection current theory in the 1930s.
All three statements correctly describe Holmes’s convection-current mechanism: radioactive heat drives convection, rising limbs split crust at ridges, and sinking limbs drag plates toward trenches.
Holmes’s theory supplied a possible driving mechanism for the continental drift theory proposed by
Alfred Wegener

secs.t: Fold mountains - young vs old, Tertiary orogeny ranges

x: The Himalayas formed from Tethyan sediments, experienced uplift during the stated epochs, began forming about 70 million years ago, continue to rise, and include the youngest Siwalik range.
The Indian Plate first moved northward, collided with Eurasia and closed the Tethys, after which its sediments were folded and thrust upward; Himalayan uplift continues today.

secs.t: Faulting - normal, reverse, thrust, block mountains, rift valleys, horst and graben

x: Satpura is a block mountain, the Narmada and Tapi occupy rift valleys, and the Vosges and Rhine Valley represent horst and graben features respectively.
The East African Rift and Rio Grande Rift illustrate normal faulting; Himalayan thrusts illustrate reverse or low-angle thrust faulting; and the San Andreas is a strike-slip fault.

secs.t: Folding - anticline, syncline, overfold, nappe

x: Compression bends rock layers and produces
folds
With increasing pressure, folds generally progress from symmetrical to asymmetrical, then overfold, recumbent fold and finally nappe.
A nappe is a recumbent fold that has been broken by a thrust and pushed far forward.
The Siwaliks consist of
simple anticline-syncline folds of the Jura type
, associated with the Alps.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The observed episode involved a 4-metre sinking of the seafloor, more than 1 metre of spreading and the eruption of 160 million cubic metres of lava over 16 days.
The observed rapid episode of sinking, spreading and lava emplacement suggested that sea-floor spreading can occur in bursts rather than at a uniform rate.

rows.title: Folding, faulting, mountain building; isostasy

secs.t: Fold mountain age groups → examples and odd-one-out

x: Exam angle: APPSC G2 2024 - of Appalachians, Aravallis, Alps, Urals, only the
Alps
are young fold mountains.
The
Himalayas, Alps and Andes
are young fold mountains associated with the Tertiary or Alpine orogeny.
Young fold mountains such as the Himalayas and Alps have
rugged relief and high conical peaks

secs.t: Block mountains and rift valleys - horst, graben → location

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2024 - "Vosges - Central Asia - fold" and "Alps - block" are wrong pairs; Appalachians (fold, N. America) and Andes (fold, S. America) are right.
The Vosges in France and the Black Forest in Germany are horsts flanking the Rhine rift valley, which is a graben.

secs.t: Diastrophism - orogenic vs epeirogenic

x: Orogenic movements are mountain-building movements caused mainly by horizontal or tangential forces and involve folding and faulting in narrow belts.
The Peninsular Block largely escaped folding but experienced vertical movements such as transgression and regression, representing an
epeirogenic effect
Orogeny produces mountain belts through predominantly horizontal forces, whereas epeirogeny produces broad continental uplift or warping through predominantly vertical or radial forces.

secs.t: Mountain types → examples; type holding the highest peaks

x: Fujiyama, Etna and Kilimanjaro are volcanic mountains; the Eastern Ghats are residual mountains; and the Black Forest is a block mountain.
The world’s highest peaks, including Mount Everest in the Himalaya, occur in
young fold mountains

secs.t: Folds - types

x: All four descriptions are correct: isoclinal limbs are parallel, an overturned limb passes beyond the vertical, a recumbent fold is nearly horizontal, and a nappe is a strongly displaced recumbent fold.
The Siwaliks display simple anticline–syncline folds of the Jura type.

secs.t: Isostasy - Airy vs Pratt

x: Isostasy refers to the gravitational balance of crustal blocks floating on denser underlying material.
Airy’s model explains relief through variations in crustal thickness at broadly uniform density, with mountains having deep roots.

secs.t: Geosyncline theory - proponent and stages

x: The sequence is lithogenesis, involving sedimentation; orogenesis, involving folding and mountain building; and gliptogenesis, involving uplift and denudation.
The rigid forelands or kratogens on either side of the geosyncline squeeze the accumulated sediments and contribute to mountain building.
The Himalaya arose through the uplift of the Tethys geosyncline during the Tertiary or Aryan era.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Supreme Court accepted the uniform definitions and paused new mining leases in November 2025, while the MoEF&CC ordered a complete ban on new leases on 24 December 2025.
Collapsing hanging glaciers in high-seismicity Himalayan zones can trigger GLOFs and landslide-lake outburst floods.

Khondalite and charnockite are associated with the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt; the Eastern Ghats constitute a major mountain belt and mineral hub of Andhra Pradesh, while Cuddapah basin sediments lie in synclinal troughs.

rows.title: Volcanoes - types, materials, landforms, global distribution

secs.t: Volcanoes in India → location and status

x: Exam angle: the APPSC GS 2021 key gives "Barren island" for mud volcanoes - the correct answer is
Baratang
; Barren is the magmatic active volcano.
The Deccan Traps are fissure or flood-basalt outpourings on the Maharashtra Plateau that occurred at the end of the Cretaceous and are linked to the Reunion hotspot.

secs.t: Magma vs lava, chamber, vent, crater, caldera; monitoring instruments

x: Magma is molten rock below the Earth's surface, usually in a magma chamber.
A caldera is a cauldron-shaped depression formed when a large eruption empties the magma chamber and the summit collapses.
A
crater
is the funnel-shaped mouth at the top of a volcano.
A
tiltmeter
measures ground tilt over faults and volcanoes.

secs.t: Distribution - belts

x: The
Pacific Ring of Fire
has the greatest concentration of volcanic eruptions and earthquakes.
Stromboli belongs to the Mediterranean volcanic belt.

secs.t: Materials - lava types, pyroclasts, gases

x: Acidic or felsic lava is silica-rich and viscous, making eruptions more explosive.
Basic or mafic lava is silica-poor and fluid, so it can flow over large distances.
Pyroclastic flows and lahars, or volcanic mudflows, are associated particularly with
stratovolcanoes
Water vapour
is the most abundant volcanic gas, followed by carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide.

secs.t: Extrusive features - lava plateaus, geysers, hot springs → state

x: Basaltic lava plateaus such as the Deccan weather to form
fertile black soil
Manikaran is a hot spring and geothermal site in the Kullu Valley of Himachal Pradesh.
Taptapani is a hot spring and geothermal site located in
Odisha
Vajreshwari is a geothermal site in
Maharashtra
Puga Valley and Chumathang are geothermal sites in
Ladakh

secs.t: Types - active, dormant, extinct; shield, composite, cinder cone

x: A dormant volcano remains quiet for a long period but may erupt again; it is not necessarily erupting at present, making statement 3 false.
Shield volcanoes are broad and have gentle slopes because they are built by relatively fluid basaltic lava.
Composite or stratovolcanoes are steep, consist of alternating lava and ash layers, and are associated with explosive eruptions.
A
cinder cone
is a small, steep cone made of loose pyroclasts.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The renewed eruption of Guatemala's Volcan de Fuego is associated with the Cocos Plate subducting beneath the Caribbean Plate.
The first three-dimensional image of Popocatepetl showed magma pools extending down to approximately
18 km
ONGC drilled India's first and deepest geothermal wells at Puga Valley in Ladakh to a depth of 1,000 metres for a 1 MW pilot project.

rows.title: Earthquakes - causes, seismic waves, measurement, distribution, effects
sub: Group-II S2-6: Earthquakes and volcanoes - causes, types, distribution and effects

secs.t: Measurement - magnitude vs intensity, scales and instruments

x: Exam angle: "Richter scale measures intensity" is wrong - it measures
magnitude
; earthquakes still cannot be predicted accurately.
Exam angle: magnitude = energy at the focus; intensity = effect at a place.
An increase of one magnitude unit on the Richter scale represents a tenfold increase in wave amplitude and an approximately 31-fold increase in energy released.
A seismograph records and measures earthquakes; a seismometer is its sensor; a seismoscope only indicates that a tremor occurred and its time; and a tiltmeter measures ground tilt.
Despite monitoring and seismological research, earthquakes cannot yet be predicted accurately in terms of their precise time, location and magnitude.

secs.t: Focus (hypocentre) vs epicentre

x: The focus, also called the hypocentre, is the point of origin of the rupture inside the Earth.
The focus is an underground point where rupture begins and may be shallow or deep; it is not located at the surface.
Rare continental mantle earthquakes originate
80 km or more below the Moho
, whereas ordinary crustal earthquakes commonly begin at depths of about 10–29 km.

secs.t: Causes - plate boundary, intraplate, reservoir-induced, volcanic

x: A tectonic earthquake occurs when stress accumulated on a fault exceeds the strength of the rocks, causing rupture and the release of seismic waves.
The Latur earthquake occurred far from a plate boundary and showed that stable continental regions can experience earthquakes along concealed or old faults.
A seismic doublet consists of two independent earthquakes of similar magnitude occurring in quick succession and close together.
The Venezuelan seismic doublet consisted of earthquakes of magnitude 7.1 and 7.5 in quick succession near the Caribbean–South American strike-slip boundary.
Seismic seiches are standing waves that may develop in enclosed or partly enclosed water bodies such as rivers, reservoirs and ponds.

secs.t: Major earthquakes → place, year, setting

x: The 2015 Gorkha earthquake in Nepal had a magnitude of 7.8, occurred along the Main Himalayan Thrust and caused liquefaction in parts of the Gangetic plain.
The February 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquake, of magnitude 7.8, occurred along the
East Anatolian Fault
between the Anatolian and Arabian plates.
The 2025 Mandalay earthquake had a magnitude of 7.7 and occurred along the Sagaing Fault, a strike-slip boundary involving the Indian and Eurasian plates.

secs.t: Himalaya-Arakan Yoma belt; seismic zones of India

x: Exam angle: "Which State/UT has no area in Zone V?" Answer: Andhra Pradesh.
In Myanmar, the
Sagaing Fault
marks the continuation of the Indian–Eurasian boundary through the eastern part of the seismic belt.
Earthquake vulnerability in India is associated with Himalayan and North-Eastern regions, liquefaction-prone alluvial plains, peninsular faults and the Andaman and Nicobar region.
Delhi, the rest of the Himalayan foothills and the Indo-Gangetic belt are cited as examples of
Zone IV
, the high-risk zone.
After the 1993 Latur earthquake, Zone I was merged into
Zone II
, resulting in the four-zone classification under IS 1893:2002.
The 2025 revision introduced a new top Zone VI for parts of Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch, and placed more than 60% of India’s landmass in moderate-to-high zones.
The 2025 revision was withdrawn after MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA objected to the cost implications.
The withdrawn map was prepared by IIT-Madras for NDMA using PSHA, 69,519 events, 36 seismogenic zones and PGA values of 0.15–0.75 g.
Zone V includes the
entire North-East, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, north Bihar, Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
The Indo-Gangetic plain, including Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal, is highly prone to
soil liquefaction
during earthquakes.

secs.t: Seismic monitoring in India

x: The network detects every Indian earthquake of magnitude 3.0 or above and global earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or above, including tsunami-capable events.
The Geological Survey of India tracks crustal strain through 34 GNSS stations.
The MoES app RISEQ is now called “
Bhookamp
.” IndiaQuake is the public-alert app of the National Centre for Seismology.
The NCS’s
IndiaQuake
app provides public earthquake alerts.

secs.t: Seismic waves - order, motion, damage

x: S-waves involve shear motion perpendicular to the direction of travel and propagate only through solids.
Love and Rayleigh waves move along the Earth's surface and are classified as
surface waves
Since S-waves cannot travel through liquids, their absence beyond the shadow zone supports the conclusion that the outer core is liquid.

secs.t: World distribution

x: The
Circum-Pacific belt
, also called the Ring of Fire, contains the world's greatest concentration of earthquakes and is associated largely with subduction around the Pacific basin.
The Pacific Ring of Fire is linked to subduction, the Mid-Atlantic belt to a divergent ridge, the Mediterranean-Himalayan belt to continental collision, and hotspots to mantle plumes.

secs.t: Effects - tsunami, landslides, liquefaction, fires

x: A tsunami generally requires an earthquake of magnitude greater than 6.5, a focus shallower than approximately 70 km and vertical uplift of the sea floor.
Earthquakes trigger landslides in the fragile Himalaya and North-East, liquefaction in soft Indo-Gangetic soils, seiches in lakes and reservoirs, and fires through broken gas and power lines.

secs.t: Volcanic landforms - intrusive and extrusive

x: Exam angle: APPSC G1 2024 - "phacoliths are large domed mounds" is the wrong statement; domes are laccoliths.
Dyke
s are vertical walls that cut across rock beds and fed the fissure eruptions associated with the Deccan Traps in western Maharashtra.
The Ladakh Magmatic Arc formed through subduction of the Neo-Tethys plate beneath Eurasia and experienced a batholith phase from approximately 160 Ma to less than 45 Ma.
Lava plateau
s, cinder and composite cones, craters, calderas and lava flows are extrusive volcanic landforms.

secs.t: World volcanoes - country and status

x: Mount St. Helens is an active stratovolcano in the Cascades of the USA, known for its 1980 eruption.
Etna is Europe's largest and most active volcano, is approximately 3,300 m high and has been a UNESCO site since 2013.
Mount
Vesuvius
is an active volcano in Italy and buried Pompeii in AD 79.
Ojos del Salado
in Chile is the world's highest active volcano, with an elevation of 6,893 m.
All three statements are correct: Volcan de Fuego is Guatemala's most active stratovolcano, has frequent Strombolian eruptions and erupted again in June 2026.

secs.t: Volcanic products and types

x: Volcanic gases consist mostly of
water vapour
, followed by carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide.
Mauna Loa
is a shield volcano formed by fluid basaltic lava and characterised by gentle slopes.
Complex or compound volcanoes contain
several vents, overlapping cones and lava domes
Strombolian eruptions involve frequent, mild bursts of bombs and ash, whereas Vulcanian eruptions are more explosive.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The M 4.4 earthquake near Koraput–Jeypore in Odisha, at a depth of 5 km, shook Araku and Paderu in the ASR district.
The withdrawn map was based on
69,519 events and 36 seismogenic zones
Experts argued that the restored 2016 hazard values were
too low for the Himalaya
The first pillar begins with construction according to IS 1893, IS 4326 and IS 13920, together with retrofitting priority buildings.
Andhra Pradesh is mainly in Zones II and III, but tremors associated with reservoirs and old Eastern Ghats faults cannot be ruled out.

rows.title: Weathering, mass wasting and soil formation; denudation and the cycle of erosion

secs.t: Soil formation - factors; active vs passive

x: Parent material
is a passive factor of soil formation, whereas climate and biological activity are active factors.
Andhra Pradesh soils are influenced by climate, altitude, bedrock composition, rainfall and heat, as well as river silt from the Godavari, Krishna and Pennar.
Andhra Pradesh soil formation reflects climate, altitude, bedrock and river deposits, while its soils mainly comprise sand, silt and clay.

secs.t: Weathering - physical, chemical, biological

x: Carbonation
occurs when carbon dioxide in rainwater forms carbonic acid, which dissolves limestone and converts carbon into bicarbonate.
Plant roots, burrowing animals, lichens and micro-organisms all break down or decay rocks and therefore contribute to biological weathering.
Heat accelerates chemical reactions and moisture supports them, making weathering fastest in hot, wet climates.

secs.t: Zonal and residual soils → region; in-situ vs transported

x: Podzol
develops under cold taiga or boreal conifer forests and is generally thin, acidic, strongly leached and humus-poor.
In hot, high-rainfall regions, intense leaching removes silica and lime from laterite and concentrates
iron and aluminium oxides
Residual or in-situ soil forms where the parent rock weathers.
Alluvium, a transported soil, covers approximately
of India.

secs.t: Mass wasting - types and terrain

x: Debris flow or mudflow
is a rapid water–soil–rock mixture commonly triggered by heavy rainfall or snowmelt.
Mass wasting is especially common on slopes steeper than 30 degrees, where rocks are weak or fractured and slopes are bare.
The southwest monsoon makes rainfall the main trigger of mass wasting in India, while earthquakes are the next major trigger.

secs.t: Cycle of erosion - Davis vs Penck; peneplain, monadnock, inselberg

x: Davis proposed the sequence of youth, maturity and old age, culminating in a low, almost flat peneplain.
Monadnocks
are resistant residual hills that remain above the nearly level surface of a peneplain in Davis’s model.
Inselbergs are residual island-hills characteristic of arid and semi-arid regions, formed through desert erosion by wind and sheet-wash.

secs.t: Soil texture - particle size, water holding, leaching

x: Sand particles are largest, followed by silt and then clay: sand (2–0.05 mm), silt (0.05–0.002 mm) and clay below 0.002 mm.
Fine-textured soils retain more water, sand drains well, and clay binds organic carbon more effectively than sandy soil.
Heavy rainfall leaches nutrients from rainforest soils, while the warm, wet conditions cause dead organic matter to decompose rapidly.

secs.t: Weathering landforms

x: Exfoliation domes develop through
onion-like peeling of granite
, commonly associated with weathering and pressure or temperature effects.
Tors are piles or groups of granite blocks.

secs.t: Denudation - sequence

x: Denudation proceeds through weathering, mass wasting or erosion, transportation and finally deposition.
Water
is considered the most powerful agent of denudation, although wind, ice and gravity also contribute.
Both statements are true, and the sequence given in the Reason explains how denudation includes preparation, removal, movement and deposition of material.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Soil biodiversity loss is ranked
fourth
among the seven threats, after erosion, loss of soil organic carbon and nutrient mismanagement.
The study found that steep, glacier-fed Himalayan catchments release CO2 through
pyrite oxidation
Water is identified as the most powerful agent of soil erosion; sheet, rill and gully are forms of water erosion, while wind erosion dominates in the Thar.

src: Sources: APSES 2024-25 p.50; CDI (Block14 AP Geography - Soils of AP; Block05 AP SES 2025-26 Complete Analysis; Block07 Pollution and Erosion; Block06 Landslides); APP (AP Geography > Soils; Indian Geography Part 1 > Soils of India, Peninsular Plateau, Rock Cycle); UPSC (Indian Geography p.119-120; Environment p.26); LENS Jul 2025 p.116, Nov 2025 p.77; LENSD 3 Sep 2026; TH 13 Sep 2026

rows.title: Major landforms - fluvial landforms and river profiles

secs.t: Depositional landforms of rivers - fans, levees, floodplains, braided channels, deltas, oxbows, terraces

x: An alluvial fan forms where a river emerges from steep hills and loses velocity, depositing coarse material in a fan-shaped spread.
Deposition on the concave side of a meander can steepen and narrow the loop until it is cut off, leaving stagnant water known as an oxbow lake.
The outer, concave bend experiences erosion and forms a cliff, whereas the inner, convex slip-off side receives deposition.

secs.t: River profile - upper, middle, lower course features

x: The youthful upper course has a steep gradient and strong vertical erosion, producing V-shaped valleys, gorges, canyons, waterfalls, rapids and potholes.
The middle course is marked by lateral erosion, transport, widening valleys and the development of meanders.
The lower or old-age course has a gentle gradient and is dominated by deposition, producing broad floodplains, levees and oxbow lakes.

secs.t: Gorge vs canyon (Grand Canyon)

x: A gorge is a deep valley with very steep or straight sides and nearly equal width at top and bottom.
Statement 4 reverses the relationship: a canyon is a variant of a gorge, not the reverse.
The Dihang gorge is associated with the
Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon near Namcha Barwa
, where the Brahmaputra enters India.

secs.t: Ravines and badland topography → region

x: Exam angle: badland region picked from options (Chambal vs Rann of Kutch, Godavari delta, western coastal plain).
Overland flow first gathers into rills; the rills merge, deepen into gullies, and a dense network of gullies produces badland topography.
A gully is a water-worn channel of semi-arid areas formed when overland flow gathers into rills that merge and deepen.

secs.t: Delta types → river examples, largest delta, conditions for formation

x: A
bird's-foot delta
has long, branching distributaries projecting into the sea; the Mississippi is the standard example given.
Delta formation depends on adequate sediment load, shallow sea, weak tides and currents, and sufficiently slow deposition-friendly flow; therefore every river does not form a delta.
The west-flowing Deccan rivers commonly have steep gradients, hard-rock channels and short courses, conditions that favour estuaries rather than extensive deltas.

secs.t: Erosional landforms (V-shaped valley, waterfall, potholes, incised meanders)

x: Eddies rotate rock fragments in depressions, causing abrasion that drills circular potholes into the bedrock.
A waterfall may form where differential resistance creates a resistant rock band or where a fault produces a step in the river profile.
When uplift rejuvenates a river, renewed vertical erosion may incise pre-existing meanders deeply into resistant bedrock.

secs.t: Drainage patterns → examples

x: Dendritic
drainage develops over relatively uniform rock and resembles the branching form of a tree; it is characteristic of the northern plains.
Trellis drainage develops in folded terrain, with tributaries commonly joining the main streams at right angles; the Appalachians provide an example.
Rectangular drainage develops where joints and faults guide stream courses, producing frequent right-angle bends, especially on joint-controlled plateaus.

secs.t: Stream capture, graded profile, base level terms

x: In stream capture, headward erosion allows one stream to breach the divide of a neighbouring basin and divert the upper course of the captured stream.
Lakes and dams can provide local base levels, while sea level is the ultimate base level; therefore all three can be base-level controls in the stated sense.
Young, rugged Himalayan relief produces sharp drainage divides, whereas prolonged erosion on old plateaus tends to make divides less distinct or faint.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The seven listed major deltas account for about 57% of the sinking delta area; deltas cover about 1% of land, support about 6% of people and contain 10 of 34 megacities.
Excessive groundwater extraction and reduced sediment or silt supply are identified as the main causes of delta sinking.
The Kolleru Wildlife Sanctuary figure cited in the APSES 2024–25 annexure is 308.55 sq km, while older material gives 250 sq km.

rows.title: Major landforms - glacial, arid/aeolian, karst and coastal landforms
sub: Group-II S2-7: Major landforms and their features - fluvial, glacial, arid, karst and coastal

secs.t: Landform → geomorphic agent (delta, cirque, cliff, sand dunes, moraine, till, hanging valley, stalactite)

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2023 matched Delta - running water, Cirque - glaciers, Cliffs - waves and currents, Sand dunes - winds.
A doline is a solutional depression produced by groundwater action in limestone, not by a glacier.
Till, moraine and boulder clay are deposits of
glacial activity
Gorges, canyons and levees are landforms associated with
running water
, particularly river erosion and deposition.

secs.t: Karst features (sinkholes, blind valleys, uvalas, stalactites vs stalagmites) and coast types (Dalmatian)

x: A sinkhole is a small depression; several sinkholes may form a doline, several dolines may merge into a uvala, and a polje is a much larger depression often related to cave collapse.
A stream lost through cracks in a karst region is called a
sinking creek
; an open-topped sinking creek is termed a boga.

secs.t: Caves → state, rock type, district (Arwah; AP: Belum, Borra, Undavalli, Bojjannakonda, Erravaram) - which are karst

x: Belum Caves are developed in black limestone and contain stalactites and stalagmites, reflecting their karst nature.
Borra Caves are karstic limestone caves through which the Gosthani flows; Mesolithic paintings are reported there, and their discovery is dated to 1807 in the cited account.
Robert Bruce Foote is associated with the first discovery of Belum Caves in 1884, while
H. D. Gebauer
mapped them during 1982–84.
Belum Caves are in Nandyal district, are black-limestone caves, rank second in natural cave length after Krem Liat Prah, and were discovered by Robert Bruce Foote in 1884.
Undavalli Caves are a rock-cut, four-storey complex near Vijayawada in Guntur district, associated with the Vishnukundins and dated to the fourth–fifth centuries CE.

secs.t: Glacial - cirque, arete, horn, U-valley, hanging valley, moraines, till, drumlins, eskers

x: A
horn
is a pointed peak formed when cirques cut back from several sides; the Matterhorn is a classic example.
Lateral, terminal, medial and ground moraines represent different positions or forms of unsorted glacial debris, and all four descriptions are correct.
An
esker
is a sinuous ridge of stratified sediment marking the course of a sub-glacial meltwater tunnel.

secs.t: Coastal erosion - agents compared, cliffs, sea caves, arches, stacks, wave-cut platforms

x: Hydraulic action
is erosion caused by the impact and pressure of water, including compressed air in coastal rock joints.
The usual sequence is cliff and wave-cut platform, sea cave, arch, stack and finally stump.
Harbours, sand mining, offshore dredging and dams can all disturb or reduce the natural supply and movement of coastal sediment.

secs.t: Aeolian - deflation hollows, mushroom rocks, yardangs, barchans, loess, playas

x: A
deflation hollow
is produced by the wind lifting and removing loose fine particles, leaving a depression.
Wind-driven sand is concentrated near the ground and abrades the base more than the upper part, producing an undercut mushroom rock.
All four pairs are correct: the Loess Plateau is in China, Normandy has Sahara-derived loess, Manchuria has Mongolia-derived loess, and Uluru is an example of an inselberg.

secs.t: Coastal depositional - beaches, spits, bars, lagoons, tombolos

x: A
beach
is the zone of sand or shingle between the low- and high-tide limits.
A
tombolo
is a depositional bar or ridge connecting an island with the mainland.
An estuary remains connected to the sea, whereas a lagoon is partly or substantially cut off; .
Groynes interrupt longshore drift and trap sediment on the updrift side.

secs.t: Fluvial landforms → river course stage; delta types

x: A gorge is nearly equal in width at the top and bottom, whereas a canyon has step-like sides and is wider at the top
V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, potholes and rapids are all characteristic features of the youthful or upper course of a river.
The Nile and Sundarbans are examples of arcuate deltas, Tiber represents a cuspate delta, and the Mississippi represents a bird-foot delta.

secs.t: Regional landform terms - doab, bhabar, khadar, badland; plain types

x: Bhabar
is the coarse gravel and pebble belt at the foothills where Himalayan rivers enter the plains.
The Terai lies south of the Bhabar and is a marshy, forested belt where streams that disappeared into the Bhabar come back to the surface.
A peneplain is a nearly featureless surface produced by prolonged erosion, and the Peninsular Plateau is described as a
rejuvenated peneplain

secs.t: Coastal landforms and coast types

x: A fiord is a drowned glacial valley, a ria is a drowned river valley, and a Dalmatian coast runs parallel to drowned ranges.
Norway has fiord coasts, north-western Spain has ria coasts, and the Adriatic coast of Croatia is a Dalmatian coast.
The east coast is soft, low-lying and largely alluvial, and its flat wide plains allow inland movement of the sea.

secs.t: Weathering and mass wasting

x: Solution, carbonation and oxidation
are chemical weathering processes.
Physical weathering causes breakdown without chemical change.
In Andhra Pradesh, weathering of granite and gneiss gives rise to
red soil
s.
Mass wasting includes soil creep, slump, landslide, mudflow and rockfall, all of which occur under the influence of
gravity

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The collapse of hanging glaciers can generate ice-rock avalanches, LLOFs and GLOFs.
Erra Matti Dibbalu comprises late-Quaternary red dunes in Visakhapatnam, while Tirumala Silathoranam is a quartzite arch more than 1.5 billion years old.
Erra Matti Dibbalu and Tirumala Silathoranam were among seven natural sites added to UNESCO's Tentative List.

rows.title: Atmosphere - structure (layers) and composition
sub: Group-II S2-8: Structure and composition of the atmosphere

secs.t: Layers → height, temperature trend, features; basis of layering

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2025 - meteorites burn up in the
mesosphere
(not thermosphere/ionosphere).
The troposphere averages about 13 km, reaches about 18 km at the equator, and contains most atmospheric water vapour, dust and clouds.
Unlike the troposphere, the temperature in the stratosphere
rises with height
, mainly because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation.

secs.t: Phenomena → layer (weather, ozone, meteors, aurora, radio waves, jet aircraft)

x: Weather occurs in the troposphere, ozone is concentrated in the stratosphere, meteors burn in the mesosphere, and auroras occur in the thermosphere or ionosphere.
The
ionosphere
, a region within the upper atmosphere and thermosphere, reflects radio waves and facilitates long-distance radio communication.
Jet aircraft commonly cruise near the base of the stratosphere because the air is relatively calm and free from most clouds and turbulence.

secs.t: Ozone layer - altitude, protective role, depleting substances, unit

x: Halocarbons such as CFCs and HCFCs release chlorine and bromine atoms that destroy ozone faster than it can form.
The Antarctic ozone hole develops mainly from
August to November
, during the Southern Hemisphere spring, aided by polar stratospheric clouds.
India achieved the stated HCFC-141b phase-out, exceeded its HCFC reduction target by January 2020, and launched the India Cooling Action Plan in March 2019 with a 2037–38 horizon.
Ultraviolet radiation splits O2 into free oxygen atoms; these combine with O2 to form O3, which absorbs UV and can split back into oxygen molecules and atoms.
The 2016 Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol provides for the phase-down of HFCs, which do not deplete ozone but have high global-warming potential.

secs.t: Composition - gases by volume, variable constituents and their distribution

x: Dust is concentrated in the lower atmospheric layers and is more abundant in
subtropical and temperate belts
, where dry winds help raise and transport particles.
Dust particles serve as hygroscopic nuclei around which water vapour can condense, assisting cloud formation.

State of the Global Climate is published by WMO; the Global Annual to Decadal Update is led by WMO with the UK Met Office; the Greenhouse Gas Bulletin is by WMO; and the Emissions Gap Report is by UNEP.

secs.t: Tropopause, stratopause, mesopause - height variation, troposphere thickness

x: Strong heating at the equator generates powerful convection currents that carry heat upward, making the tropopause higher there.
The normal lapse rate is a fall of about 1°C for every 165 m of ascent, equivalent to approximately 6.5°C per kilometre.
Under normal conditions, temperature decreases at about 6.5°C for every kilometre increase in height.

secs.t: Homosphere vs heterosphere - sub-layers

x: The homosphere has a relatively uniform mixture, while the heterosphere has gases arranged in layers by molecular weight.
The heterosphere is described as having nitrogen, atomic oxygen, helium and hydrogen in upward order according to molecular weight.
The homosphere comprises the
troposphere, stratosphere and mesosphere

secs.t: Ionosphere sub-layers (D, E, F) and communication role

x: The ionosphere contains charged particles that reflect radio waves back to Earth, making long-distance communication possible.
Solar flares and geomagnetic storms can disturb ionospheric conditions and disrupt
GNSS signals
The D layer absorbs medium and long waves, the E layer reflects medium-frequency radio waves, and the F layer is the main reflector of short-wave radio.

secs.t: Temperature trend in each layer (reversal layers)

x: The stratospheric and thermospheric temperature increases are inversion trends caused by absorption of radiation, while temperature falls through the mesosphere.
The
stratosphere and thermosphere
are reversal layers in which temperature increases with height, unlike the normal decrease in the troposphere and mesosphere.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The method maps
the topside ionosphere
over India up to 1,000 km and is intended to improve NavIC and GPS accuracy.
The atmosphere is relatively transparent to incoming solar radiation but absorbs outgoing terrestrial radiation, thereby contributing to the greenhouse effect.
The 2025 ozone hole peaked at just over 21 million square kilometres, well
below the 2006 record of 29 million square kilometres
, and closed early.

rows.title: Insolation and heat budget; horizontal and vertical distribution of temperature, inversion
sub: Group-II S2-9: Insolation, heat budget and the distribution of temperature

secs.t: Heating/cooling processes → mechanism (conduction, convection, advection, radiation)

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2023 matched Advection - horizontal, Convection - vertical, Insolation - direct, Conduction - lower layers.
The Loo transfers heat horizontally through moving air and is therefore an example of
advection
Convection is vertical movement of heat: warm, less-dense air rises and cooler air sinks.
Conduction transfers heat through direct
particle-to-particle contact
and is most effective in solids.

secs.t: Albedo → surface ranking; role of high and low clouds

x: High, thin clouds tend to trap outgoing heat and cause warming, whereas low, thick clouds reflect more incoming sunlight and cause cooling.
Approximately 35 of every 100 units received at the top of the atmosphere are reflected back to space, giving an overall planetary albedo of about
35 percent
Melting ice exposes dark ocean water, which has a lower albedo and absorbs more heat, producing a positive ice-albedo feedback.

secs.t: Heat budget - greenhouse effect, short-wave vs long-wave, what heats the atmosphere directly

x: The atmospheric absorption of the 34 units consists of 6 units by direct radiation, 9 by convection and turbulence, and 19 as latent heat of condensation.
The atmosphere permits much incoming short-wave radiation to pass but absorbs outgoing long-wave, or infrared, terrestrial radiation and re-radiates part of it.
On the stated 100-year scale, carbon dioxide has a GWP of 1, methane 28–36 and nitrous oxide 265–298.
Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation and re-radiate part of it back toward the surface, raising Earth's temperature.

secs.t: Horizontal distribution - isotherms in January vs July, land-sea contrast

x: In January, Northern Hemisphere isotherms bend equatorward over colder landmasses and poleward over relatively warmer oceans.
Land heats more rapidly than water, so summer temperatures over continents are relatively higher and the isotherms bend poleward over land.
Isotherms connect places of equal temperature, generally follow an east-west direction, and are more regular in the ocean-dominated Southern Hemisphere.

secs.t: Annual and diurnal range - continental vs maritime, latitude of minimum range, clear vs cloudy nights

x: Continental interiors at high latitudes experience very hot summers and very cold winters, producing a large annual range; Siberia is a standard example.
The annual range is generally minimum
at the Equator
because seasonal changes in solar altitude and day length are small.
Clear skies allow greater radiational loss of heat from the Earth, whereas clouds send some outgoing heat back toward the surface.

secs.t: Vertical distribution - normal lapse rate and why temperature falls with height

x: The ground heats the atmosphere from below.
Solar radiation is primarily short-wave, while the Earth re-emits absorbed energy as long-wave infrared radiation.
Earth's outgoing long-wave infrared radiation is approximately in the 8,000–25,000 nanometre range.

secs.t: Insolation - factors and latitudinal distribution

x: The angle of the rays, duration of sunshine, atmospheric transparency, and slope and aspect of land all influence insolation.
The Equator receives the most annual insolation, whereas maximum insolation at a given time or region is associated with the relatively cloudless subtropical deserts.
Concrete and asphalt absorb and retain heat, causing urban areas to be warmer than their rural surroundings.

secs.t: Temperature inversion - conditions, types, effects

x: Long winter nights, clear skies, calm and dry air, and snow cover favour rapid surface cooling and inversion formation.
Cold, dense air flows downslope and accumulates in valleys, producing frost pockets while the slopes remain relatively warmer.
Cold air settles on valley floors during an inversion, making upper slopes relatively warmer and more suitable for orchards and plantations.

secs.t: Thermal equator, urban heat islands, hottest/coldest places

x: Both statements are true, and the seasonal apparent movement of the Sun causes the line of highest mean temperature to shift.
Chennai's vegetation reportedly declined from 25% in 2014 to 10% in 2024, while built-up area increased from 36% to 67%.
Lambasingi in ASR district is regarded as the coldest place in Andhra Pradesh, with temperatures of about 2°C, and is called the ‘Kashmir of AP’.

secs.t: Range of temperature - by latitude, interior vs coast, hottest latitudes

x: Continentality
causes large annual and daily temperature ranges in continental interiors, while maritime influence moderates temperature near coasts.
Sub-tropical deserts around 20°–30° N have
clear skies and dry air
, permitting very high temperatures; the Equator does not record the highest temperatures merely because it receives strong insolation.
In winter, the 20°C isotherm extends from the mouth of the Tapi to the Mahanadi delta.

secs.t: Heat waves - IMD criteria and AP districts

x: For plains, the threshold temperature to qualify for a heat wave is
. The 45°C value is the separate actual-maximum criterion for plains.
The threshold maximum temperatures are 40°C for plains, 37°C for coasts and 30°C for hills.
A departure
above 6.4°C
from the normal temperature constitutes a severe heat wave; 4.5°C to 6.4°C corresponds to a heat wave.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: TRISHNA is an Indo-French mission involving
ISRO and CNES
, intended to track land-surface temperature and urban heat islands; its launch is associated with 2027.
A heat dome
drove the record early heatwave in Western Europe by allowing heat to persist under stalled high pressure.
TRISHNA is a thermal-infrared mission for land-surface temperature, energy and water budgets, and urban heat islands; it is not designed only for visible-light cyclone tracking.
