rows.title: Andhra Pradesh - drainage: Godavari, Krishna, Penna, Vamsadhara, Nagavali; reservoirs and canals
sub: Group-II S2-23: Andhra Pradesh - drainage system: Godavari, Krishna, Penna and minor rivers

secs.t: Irrigation projects, barrages and tanks → river and district

x: Exam angle: "Anantaraja Sagar / Cumbum tank is in which district / on which river".
Srisailam, Nagarjuna Sagar, Pulichintala and Prakasam Barrage are listed as Krishna basin structures at the stated locations.
Sunkesula Barrage is constructed on the
Tungabhadra River
in Kurnool district and forms the head of the KC Canal.
Veligonda conveys Krishna water from Srisailam into the Gundlakamma basin through Nallamala Sagar.
Veligonda Phase-I was stated to involve 10.70 TMC ft of water, irrigation of 1.19 lakh acres and drinking water for four lakh people.
The cost stated for the 117 new gates was
₹152.95 crore
. ₹768 crore is associated with payments to displaced Veligonda families.
The stated distribution is 66.81 lakh acres under major, 5.62 lakh acres under medium and 25.60 lakh acres under minor irrigation, totaling 106.15 lakh acres.

secs.t: Rivers → origin, states traversed, length within AP and outfall

x: Exam angle: match river → origin hills (Vamsadhara - Jayapur; Machkund - Mudugal; Gundlakamma - Nallamala; Pennar - Nandidurga).
The
Vamsadhara
is described as the biggest river rising in the Eastern Ghats.
The Gosthani originates in the Eastern Ghats, has a length of about 120 km and forms an estuary near Bheemunipatnam.
The Swarnamukhi basin includes Tirumala and Srikalahasti, Kalyani is its tributary and Mogaleru is its literary name in Dhurjati’s works.
Mahendra Tanaya, which originates in the Mahendragiri hills, is a tributary of the
Vamsadhara
The total lengths are Godavari 1,465 km, Krishna about 1,400 km, Penna 597 km and Vamsadhara 254 km.
Godavari extends about 250 km in Andhra Pradesh, Krishna about 485 km, Pennar 536 km of its 597 km lies in the State, and the Godavari reaches the sea through seven distributaries.

secs.t: Inter-state disputes, river boards and tribunals

x: Bahuda, Vamsadhara and Nagavali are covered by inter-state agreements, while Godavari waters are governed through a tribunal award.
The Bachawat Tribunal's Krishna award involved 2,060 TMC at 75% dependability, of which Andhra Pradesh's share was 811 TMC.
The Brijesh Kumar Tribunal, or KWDT-II, dealt with the Krishna dispute and submitted its report in 2010, followed by a further report in 2013.
Babli barrage is a Maharashtra barrage on the Godavari upstream of
Sriramsagar
and was disputed by undivided Andhra Pradesh.
The
Polavaram–Banakacherla link
carries surplus Godavari water through the Krishna and onward to the Penna basin.
Telangana argues that the project involves excess use of the Krishna share and violates the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 and the Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal award of 1980.

secs.t: Canals, river linking and lift schemes → purpose and beneficiaries

x: Godavari–Penna Phase-I involves 73 TMC, a five-stage lift and 7,000 cusecs; it was approximately 21% complete.
The Polavaram–Nallamala Sagar link proposes transfer of Godavari floodwater to Rayalaseema through Bollapalli.
The Nagavali–Suvarnamukhi link was about 19.32% complete and is intended to provide
drinking water to Vizianagaram
The NWDA priority link runs from Godavari at Inchampalli through Krishna at Nagarjunasagar and Pennar at Somasila to the Cauvery.
Pattiseema lifts Godavari water into the Polavaram Right Main Canal, which carries it to the Krishna at
Prakasam Barrage
Veligonda carries water from Srisailam to the Gundlakamma basin through tunnels in the Nallamala hills.
The design figures are 194.6 TMC storage, irrigation potential of 7.20 lakh acres, 960 MW generation and diversion of 80 TMC to the Krishna.
All three statements are correct: Godavari–Penna Phase-I involves 73 TMC through a five-stage lift, Package-I was reported at 21%, and Telangana opposes the proposed Polavaram–Nallamala Sagar link.

secs.t: River basin shares and longest river of AP

x: The listed Godavari basin States and region are Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and Puducherry (Yanam).
All four pairs correctly state the basin-sharing regions listed for these rivers and streams.

secs.t: River landforms - distributaries, islands, canyon, lake, confluences

x: At Dowleswaram, the Godavari splits into the two main distributaries,
Gautami and Vasishta
The seven mouths include Gautami, Vasishta, Vainateya, Tulya, Bharadwaja, Kaushika and Athreya.
Diviseema, also called Divi island, lies between the two branches of the Krishna formed at Puligadda.
Bhavani Island is a Krishna river island near
Prakasam Barrage at Vijayawada
and is used as a tourism destination.
Gandikota gorge, also called the Gandikota canyon, is formed by the Penna in
YSR Kadapa district

secs.t: Water abstraction and basin comparisons among Indian rivers

x: India has 20 river basins, comprising 12 major and 8 composite basins.
The Godavari has the largest peninsular basin, followed by the Krishna and the Mahanadi.
The
Narmada and Cauvery
basins are approximately equal in size.

secs.t: Telugu Ganga project

x: The Telugu Ganga Project takes Krishna water from Srisailam, supplies Chennai, irrigates 2.75 lakh acres in Kurnool and Kadapa, and was conceived by N. T. Rama Rao.
The route runs from Srisailam through the Penna basin at Somasila, then Kandaleru, and finally Poondi in Tamil Nadu.
10 TMC ft
was proposed to be released for Chennai’s drinking water.

secs.t: Penna system - tributaries and outfall

x: The Penna meets the sea at
Utukuru in Nellore
district.
Papagni
is a right-bank tributary of the Penna and originates from Chikkaballapur via the Nandi Hills.
The Cheyyeru is formed by the
Bahuda and Pancha
rivers.
Cheyyeru joins at Gundlamada in Kadapa and is associated with the Annamayya dam; Sagileru joins near Kamalapuram, while Chitravathi joins at Gandikota.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The reported flood situation included 5.2 lakh cusecs at Dowleswaram, approximately 521 TMC ft flowing to the sea, 150 relief camps in Polavaram district and good inflows at Gotta and Thotapalli.
The AP–Telangana dispute includes the proposed Godavari diversion associated with Banakacherla and Nallamala Sagar.
The KRMB committee limited water from
Srisailam and Nagarjunasagar
to drinking use only because of El Niño conditions.

rows.title: Andhra Pradesh - climate, rainfall regions, cyclone vulnerability, drought-prone areas
sub: Group-II S2-22: Andhra Pradesh - climate, rainfall regions and cyclone vulnerability
Group-II S2-28: Cyclone, flood, drought and tsunami management with reference to Andhra Pradesh

secs.t: Cyclone vulnerability - vulnerable districts, major cyclones → landfall

x: Exam angle: year of Hudhud (2014), state hit by Titli.
Regardless of variation in its all-India rank among sources, Andhra Pradesh has the longest coastline on the eastern coast of India and is highly exposed to Bay of Bengal cyclones.
The Diviseema cyclone struck Diviseema in the Krishna delta on 19 November 1977 and produced a huge storm surge.
Both statements are true, and the rapid communication of IMD alerts to district administrations together with preparedness explains why the Hudhud experience exemplified proactive risk governance.
Accurate warnings and timely evacuation
contributed significantly to the sharp fall in deaths during cyclones such as Phailin and Fani.

secs.t: Rainfall regions and variability - SW vs NE share, IMD report

x: Rayalaseema and the southern coastal districts
depend more on the North-East or retreating monsoon than other parts of the State.
The June–December total was 960.3 mm against a normal of 860.0 mm, representing a positive deviation of 11.7%.
During the El Niño-related 2026 season, a 27.3% deficit was reported on 23 June, and 11 of 28 districts were deficient.

secs.t: Regional disaster profile - coastal Andhra vs Rayalaseema

x: Coastal Andhra faces cyclones and related coastal hazards; Rayalaseema and southern Prakasam face chronic drought and groundwater depletion; inland plains face rising heat waves.
The coast is exposed to cyclones and storm surge, the Godavari–Krishna deltas to floods, and semi-arid Rayalaseema to drought.
Rural distress is particularly severe in drought-prone Rayalaseema and rain-fed
Prakasam, Anantapur, Kurnool and Kadapa

secs.t: Drought-prone Rayalaseema - deficit and resilience projects

x: Rayalaseema lies in the rain shadow of both
the Western and Eastern Ghats
, contributing to low and erratic rainfall.
Watershed projects may improve groundwater, but crop yields can remain flat when crop diversification and soil management are neglected.
The Kurnool initiative targeted
92,000 acres
and promoted millets, pulses, oilseeds and Jeevamrutham.

secs.t: Disaster preparedness and cyclone shelters

x: The Disaster Management Act, 2005 and the AP Disaster Management Rules, 2007 provide the stated framework.
Cyclone shelters, evacuation plans, IMD early warning, coastal shelter belts and mangroves are mitigation measures.
INCOIS at
Hyderabad
houses the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre.
Although the Andhra Pradesh coast was hit in 2004,
Tamil Nadu
was the worst-affected State.

secs.t: Temperature regime - hottest places, heat-wave districts

x: Lambasingi
in ASR district is called the “Kashmir of Andhra Pradesh” and can experience temperatures of about 2°C.
Winter is January–February, summer is March to mid-June, the south-west monsoon is mid-June to September, and the retreating monsoon is October–December.
Rentachintala in Palnadu
is identified as the hottest place in Andhra Pradesh and often records temperatures above 47°C.

secs.t: Rain-shadow and drought-prone zone

x: Both statements are true, and the rain-shadow location explains the limited south-west monsoon rainfall of Rayalaseema.
Failure of the
north-east monsoon
can cause chronic droughts in Rayalaseema and southern Prakasam.
Groundwater depletion
adds to the impact of recurring droughts in Rayalaseema and southern Prakasam.
Annamayya
recorded a deficiency of 75.9%, compared with 67.5% in Prakasam and 65% in Chittoor.

secs.t: AP climate vs neighbouring states - winter rainfall

x: The
Coromandel coast of Tamil Nadu
receives most of its rainfall from the north-east monsoon rather than the south-west monsoon.
Andhra Pradesh lies between the predominantly south-west-monsoon regime of most of India and the north-east-monsoon regime of Tamil Nadu; about one-third of its rainfall occurs in October–December.
The mostly dry winter may receive occasional light rain from
retreating systems and western disturbances

secs.t: APSDMA - statutory role, early warning, coordination, IMD Visakhapatnam

x: The City Flood Alert was developed through collaboration among
RTGS, APSDMA and IIT Gandhinagar
All four statements correctly describe the City Flood Alert: its forecast periods, technological inputs, Budameru data base and proposed extension to all ULBs.
The direction required round-the-clock control rooms at State and district levels and dissemination of IMD and APSDMA alerts to field-level agencies.

secs.t: Flood forecasting and control - CWC, expert committees, embankments, zoning

x: Flood management is a State subject, while the Centre supports States through technical guidance and promotional funding under FMBAP, which also includes anti-sea-erosion works.
Phase II covers 11 cities, including Visakhapatnam, with funding shared in the ratio of 90:10 between the Centre and the State.
Visakhapatnam
is among the 11 cities covered by Phase II of the Urban Flood Risk Management Programme.

secs.t: Drought management - Manual 2016, CDP threshold, CWWG, SC guidelines

x: Rainfall deviation and dry spells trigger the assessment, while the listed impact indicators help confirm whether drought is moderate or severe.
The Crop Weather Watch Group meets
weekly
during the monsoon to monitor rainfall, sowing and reservoir conditions.
The Supreme Court directed that the drought manual be updated and the
National Disaster Mitigation Fund
be set up.

secs.t: Cyclone mitigation - shelters, roof design, NCRMP

x: Multipurpose shelters, raised platforms, all-weather evacuation roads and storm-surge barriers are all structural cyclone-mitigation measures identified in the guidelines.
A hipped roof with firm anchoring of the roof to the walls resists high winds better than a gable roof.
NCRMP Phase I was World Bank-aided, covered Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, and formed part of the wider mitigation effort involving shelters and forecasting.

secs.t: Godavari and Krishna flood management - embankments, Polavaram

x: The Godavari Anicut is now the Sir Arthur Cotton, or Dowleswaram, Barrage near Rajamahendravaram.
The Krishna and Godavari River Management Boards advise both States on
water releases for flood and drought mitigation
under Schedule 11.
Godavari flood management during July 2026 included relief camps, deployment of NDRF and SDRF personnel, and early flood warnings.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The India Meteorological Department warned that the first cyclone of the season could form over the Andaman Sea around
19–21 September 2026
and was likely to cross the Odisha coast.
Andhra Pradesh faces the combined risks of east-coast cyclones, hazards associated with two major deltas and drought in its interior, requiring multi-hazard planning.

rows.title: Andhra Pradesh - natural vegetation and forests; forest cover and types

secs.t: District-wise forest cover - highest/lowest

x: YSR Kadapa
had the largest forest area among the pre-2022 districts.
Visakhapatnam
had the highest forest cover and Krishna had the lowest among the pre-2022 districts.
Nallamala
is the largest forest block in Andhra Pradesh.
Simhachalam lies in the north, Balaghat in the west, and Palakonda and Nallamala are southern forest hills.

secs.t: Forest fires - area affected and rank

x: Andhra Pradesh recorded the highest forest area affected by fire in India during the 2023–24 fire season.
All four locations—Horsley Hills, Mallappa Konda near Kuppam, Mallaiahkonda and the Somala belt—were identified as fire-prone zones.
Temperatures in the affected areas rose above
during April–May.

secs.t: Forest types of AP → hill range/region

x: Tropical dry deciduous forests contain
teak, Terminalia, red sanders and Anogeissus
as the principal listed species.
Araku and Paderu lie in the northern Eastern Ghats, Papikondalu has moist deciduous forests, and thorn and scrub vegetation is associated with Rayalaseema.
Teak is associated with dry deciduous forests, bamboo and sandalwood with the northern Eastern Ghats hill forests, and mangroves with Coringa, the Krishna delta and Pulicat.

secs.t: Forest programmes and diversion

x: The cumulative diverted forest land was
up to 31 December 2024; 26,924.34 ha was the figure up to 2017–18.
CAMPA funds
compensatory afforestation through an Annual Plan of Operation
The 2026 change allows commercial plantations on degraded forest land and is linked to the national goal of 33% forest cover.
The 16th Finance Commission included open forests in the devolution forest criterion using
density-based weights

secs.t: Forest density classes - VDF, MDF, OF, scrub

x: VDF covers 1,995.71 sq km, MDF 13,725.75 sq km, OF 14,363.50 sq km and scrub 8,351.62 sq km.
Rollapadu is a small grassland sanctuary, Nelapattu is a wetland, Sri Lankamalleswara lies in the Lankamala hills and Pulicat is a lagoon shared with Tamil Nadu.
All four area figures are correctly matched: Coringa 235.70, Kolleru 308.55, Papikonda 1,012.90 and Sri Venkateswara National Park 353.63 sq km.

secs.t: Valuable species → forest region

x: Red sanders is endemic to the Seshachalam, Palakonda and Veligonda ranges of Andhra Pradesh.
Red sanders is IUCN-listed as Endangered, appears in Schedule IV of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, and is included in CITES Appendix II.
Thermal-imaging drones
have been used against red sanders smuggling in the Seshachalam region.

secs.t: Forest produce and revenue

x: During April–December 2024–25,
timber production was 1,562.886 cmt against a target of 24,925.69 cmt
TRIFED was established in 1987 under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act, 1984, and functions under the Ministry of Tribal Affairs for the MSP for MFP.
APFDC is the government’s agent for exporting
red sanders wood and beedi leaf

secs.t: Plantation agencies - APFDC plantations by crop

x: The correct descending order is clonal eucalyptus (33,584 ha), cashew (5,664 ha), coffee (4,010 ha) and bamboo (2,359 ha).
Eucalyptus of seed origin covers 2,610 ha, bamboo 2,359 ha, teak 956 ha and cashew 5,664 ha.
APFDC is the largest eucalyptus grower among PSUs in India, provides about 9 lakh man-days of work annually and has 2.20 lakh pepper standards on its coffee estates.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The reported green-cover gain was 1,445 sq km, but only
156 sq km
represented true forest.
The criticism is that planting drives, including the target of 140 crore saplings under “Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam”, can increase tree cover without creating natural forests.
The Rekapalli revolt of 1879 was directed against
British forest laws

rows.title: Andhra Pradesh - national parks, wildlife sanctuaries (Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam, Coringa, Papikonda, Rollapadu, Kolleru) and Ramsar sites
sub: Group-II S2-25: Andhra Pradesh - natural vegetation, forests, national parks and sanctuaries

secs.t: Sanctuaries/NPs → flagship species

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G1 2024 match - Coringa-saltwater crocodile, Rollapadu-GIB, Sri Lankamalleswara-Jerdon's courser.
Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary is associated with the saltwater crocodile and mangrove vegetation.
The listed biodiversity highlights are red sanders, tiger, Indian bison, Great Indian Bustard and golden gecko.
Kanchu mekha, a local dwarf goat breed, is associated with
Papikonda National Park

secs.t: Protected areas → district and river/landscape

x: Exam angle: chronology of notification, sanctuary → district after the 2022 district reorganisation, species → sanctuary.
The Rajiv Gandhi Wildlife Sanctuary (Tiger Reserve) extends over
Nandyal, Prakasam and Palnadu
districts and forms part of the Nallamala landscape.
Sri Venkateswara Wildlife Sanctuary and National Park
are associated with Annamayya and Tirupati districts and the Seshachalam–Tirumala hill landscape.
Papikonda National Park lies in Eluru and Alluri Sitharama Raju districts, in the Papikondalu gorge on both banks of the Godavari.
Gundla Brahmeswaram is a dry deciduous forest sanctuary and is associated with the new critically rare herb Euphorbia chalamensis.

Cycas beddomei occurs in the Seshachalam hills, Boswellia ovalifoliolata in Andhra Pradesh, Jerdon's Courser in the Sri Lankamalleswara Wildlife Sanctuary, and the Gooty tarantula has a very restricted range in Nandyal district.

secs.t: Chronology of notification of AP sanctuaries

x: The correct sequence is Pulicat (1976), Coringa (1978), Rollapadu (1988) and Kolleru (1999).
Papikonda
Wildlife Sanctuary was upgraded to Papikonda National Park in 2008.
The Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve was notified in 2010.
The indicated order is Nelapattu, Rollapadu, Kaundinya and Kolleru.
Krishna
Wildlife Sanctuary was notified in 1989.
Kaundinya
Wildlife Sanctuary was notified in 1990.

secs.t: Tiger reserve and elephant reserve of AP

x: Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve lies in the
Nallamala hills
Tiger reserves are managed on
a core-buffer model under the National Tiger Conservation Authority
, in accordance with the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
Kaundinya Wildlife Sanctuary
is Andhra Pradesh’s only Asian elephant habitat and lies near the Tamil Nadu border.
The migration was attributed to drought in the
Hosur-Dharmapuri reserve forests and Bannerghatta
Red Sanders, tiger, Indian Bison, Great Indian Bustard and Golden Gecko are listed as flagship or endemic species; the four given statements are correct.
The NSTR-Seshachalam landscape was reported to have
68 tigers and 11 cubs

secs.t: Bird sanctuaries, IBAs and marine areas → district

x: Telineelapuram and Telukunchi are in Srikakulam, Uppalapadu is in Guntur, and Kolleru lies between the Krishna and Godavari deltas.
Uppalapadu has pelicans and painted storks, Nelapattu has a spot-billed pelican breeding colony, and Pulicat attracts very large wintering populations of greater flamingos.
The mass mortality at Telineelapuram involved the
spot-billed pelican
, Pelecanus philippensis.
The coastal wetlands of Andhra Pradesh also receive
Siberian cranes and painted storks

secs.t: Endemic/local breeds and species → protected area

x: Red Sanders is endemic to the
Seshachalam, Palakonda and Veligonda ranges
, including the Sri Venkateswara landscape.
The Golden Gecko is associated with the
Tirumala hills

secs.t: Sanctuaries of other states used as distractors

x: Grazing is not permitted inside a National Park, and alteration of its boundary requires the recommendation of the National Board for Wildlife.
Mrugavani National Park, Kasu Brahmananda Reddy National Park and Eturunagaram Wildlife Sanctuary are located in Telangana.

secs.t: Forest regions - tree species and forest type (Seshachalam, Nallamala, Palakonda)

x: Red Sanders is endemic to the
southern Eastern Ghats
of Andhra Pradesh and is characteristic of the Seshachalam and Palakonda belts.
All three regional associations are correct: Seshachalam is linked with Tirupati and Annamayya, Palakonda with Kadapa and Annamayya, and Nallamala with Nandyal, Prakasam and Palnadu.
The forest-bearing hills identified in Andhra Pradesh are
North Simhachalam, West Balaghat, South Palakonda and Nallamala

secs.t: Mangroves - Godavari and Krishna deltas, Coringa

x: Large-scale afforestation in these deltaic mangrove areas began during the
Sixth Five-Year Plan
Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary is associated with Kakinada and covers approximately 235.70 square kilometres.
The principal mangrove formations of Andhra Pradesh occur in the estuaries of the
Godavari and Krishna
rivers.
State economic survey documents describe Andhra Pradesh’s mangroves as the second-largest ecosystem, whereas ISFR 2023 places Gujarat second nationally.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The incident concerns a tiger’s movement from Papikonda and its safe return to East Godavari, representing a current human–wildlife interaction associated with a protected area.
The SES 2025–26 information reports 48 community eco-tourism centres in Andhra Pradesh.
The protected-area network of Andhra Pradesh includes India’s largest tiger reserve and the Red Sanders endemic-tree belt under special protection.

rows.title: Andhra Pradesh - soil types and their distribution
sub: Group-II S2-24: Andhra Pradesh - soils and their distribution

secs.t: Red soils - share of state area and sub-types

x: Exam angle: match red-soil sub-types with % (loamy sub-soil 30, clay base 12, red loamy 9).
Red soil
is the most extensive soil type in Andhra Pradesh and covers approximately 60–66 per cent of the State’s area.
Red earth with loamy subsoil accounts for 30 per cent, red soil with clay base for 12 per cent, red loamy soil for 9 per cent and red sandy soil for 8 per cent.
Red soils are widely distributed in Rayalaseema, including Anantapur, Sri Sathya Sai, Kadapa, Nandyal and Kurnool, and also occur in coastal uplands.

secs.t: Soil types of AP → area ranking and regions

x: Skeletal soil
s occur in minor amounts, particularly in heavily eroded tracts of Andhra Pradesh.

The three largest categories are loamy to clayey skeletal deep reddish-brown soils at 20.42 per cent, clayey to gravelly clayey moderately deep dark-brown soils at 18.65 per cent, and moderately deep calcareous black soils at 9.57 per cent.

secs.t: Laterite soils in AP - extent, formation, areas

x: Intense leaching removes silica and lime, contributing to acidity and low fertility in laterite soils.
Laterite soils are generally less fertile and poor in organic matter; their fertility is low despite the presence of iron and aluminium oxides.
Ellavaram, Peddapuram, Kavali, Kovvur, Gudur and Sullurpeta
are listed as laterite-soil areas.

secs.t: Soil synonyms → soil type

x: Regur or Regadi means black cotton soil, Vertisols are black soils, Chalka denotes red sandy soil and Bhangar denotes old alluvium.
Dubba is a local red-soil sub-type.
Bhangar refers to old alluvium, whereas Khadar refers to new alluvium.

secs.t: Black soils - districts and crops

x: Black soils are rich in calcium, potash and magnesium, but poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus; they also retain water well.
Deep cracks formed on drying loosen and turn the soil, giving black soil its
self-ploughing
character.
Black gram
is specifically identified as doing best on black soils, while mango and cashew suit lateritic soils and coffee suits hill soils.

secs.t: Deltaic alluvium - formation and delta crops

x: Floods of the major rivers deposit fresh river-borne silt, periodically renewing the deltaic alluvium.
Deltaic alluvial soil is porous and loamy, retains moisture well and is rich in potash and lime.
The Krishna-Godavari deltaic tracts are characterised by highly fertile
deltaic alluvial soil
Paddy, sugarcane, vegetables and fruits are among the crops suited to deltaic alluvial soils.

secs.t: Problem soils - saline, alkaline, acidic, waterlogged

x: Salinity lowers crop yields and may break down soil structure.
Laterite soil
s are associated with acidic conditions, whereas black soils are generally neutral to strongly alkaline.
Alkalinity
, which may result from alkaline irrigation water, reduces the availability of nutrients to plants.
Salinity affects plant water and nutrient uptake, damages soil structure and may pollute water bodies.

secs.t: Soil Health Card and soil testing

x: Soil Health Cards provide soil-sample analysis and village-wise nutrient mapping, helping farmers understand soil nutrient status.
Since 2022-23, Soil Health and Fertility has been operated under the Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (
RKVY
Since 2022–23, the scheme has been implemented as the
Soil Health and Fertility
component of the Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana.

secs.t: Soil erosion and land degradation in Rayalaseema

x: Clay soil
s hold more soil organic carbon, whereas sandy soils and steep slopes lose it through leaching and erosion.

All four area-problem pairs are correctly matched: drought and wind erosion in Anantapur and Sri Sathya Sai, coastal erosion at Uppada, salinity and waterlogging in deltas, and topsoil loss through Podu cultivation in ASR and Parvathipuram Manyam.

secs.t: Soil-crop suitability in AP

x: Paddy suits deltaic alluvium, cotton suits black soil, groundnut suits red soil and mango suits laterite soil.
Groundnut, castor and millets
are associated with red soils.
Mango and cashew are identified as crops suited to
laterite soil
s.
Coffee, tea and horticulture are associated with hill, or skeletal, soils in the ASR region.

secs.t: Saline and alkaline soils of AP - coastal districts, reclamation

x: Deltaic salinity is also associated with poor drainage, faulty irrigation and saline water intrusion; it is not caused exclusively by natural coastal processes.
The green-manure drive for Kharif 2026 involved an allocation of
₹62.20 crore and 91,918 quintals of seed
The seed component consisted of
sunn hemp, dhaincha and green gram
, which are used to help rebuild soil fertility through green manuring.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Current relevance:
AP is running a
₹62.20 crore green-manure drive
for Kharif 2026 (91,918 quintals of sunn hemp, dhaincha and green gram seed) to rebuild soil fertility.
Comparative note:
alluvium is India's most widespread soil (45.6%), but in AP red soil dominates and alluvium covers only ~6%.

rows.title: Andhra Pradesh - rocks and minerals: barytes, limestone, mica, coal, oil and gas basins (KG basin)
sub: Group-II S2-32: Natural resources of Andhra Pradesh - minerals, forests, water and marine resources

secs.t: Minerals → erstwhile district/place

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2023 match - Mica-Nellore, Coal-West Godavari, Bauxite-East Godavari; Manganese is the fourth pair (district cut off in the sample).
Chimakurthy is known for Galaxy or black granite, while Srikakulam Blue, Pista Green of Kadapa and Chilli Red of Anantapur are other noted granite varieties or localities.
Mangampeta is associated with barytes, Tummalapalle with uranium, Ramagiri with gold and Chimakurthy with Galaxy or black granite.

secs.t: Oil and gas - KG basin, refinery, operators

x: Kakinada offshore, Amalapuram/Konaseema and Krishna offshore are associated with the KG basin.
Tatipaka in Konaseema is the site of
an ONGC mini-refinery
KG-D6 is
a deepwater block off the Andhra Pradesh coast associated with Reliance Industries and BP
Mumbai Offshore, Krishna-Godavari, Assam and Cambay are all identified as major natural-gas basins in India.
JHBDPL
is associated with the Pradhan Mantri Urja Ganga gas-pipeline project.

secs.t: AP share of India's reserves/production

x: Andhra Pradesh has about 327 million tonnes out of India's 1,078 million tonnes of heavy-mineral beach sand resources, amounting to approximately 30.4%.
Andhra Pradesh is stated to have about 615 million tonnes of bauxite out of the national total, or approximately
Tummalapalle is the principal uranium locality mentioned for Andhra Pradesh, and its uranium ore is described as low-grade.

secs.t: Geological formations → minerals and region

x: Archaean
rocks, including extensive gneiss, occupy most of Andhra Pradesh and contain iron, manganese, copper, lead and gold.
The Eastern Ghats khondalite formation is associated with the
Visakhapatnam Agency
and contains bauxite, graphite and manganese.
Coastal sands containing ilmenite, rutile, zircon, garnet and monazite extend broadly from
Srikakulam to Nellore

secs.t: Gold - resource districts and private gold mine

x: The Swarnagiri mine is operated by GeoMysore Services under a 30-year lease and is located in Tuggali mandal of Kurnool district.
Gold
reserves occur at Ramagiri in Anantapur district, and gold-bearing quartz is found across parts of Rayalaseema.
Mangampeta is the barytes deposit in YSR Kadapa, Tummalapalle is the uranium mine in YSR Kadapa, and Jonnagiri is the gold mine in Kurnool.

secs.t: Barytes - deposits and India/world share

x: The state policy promotes beneficiation plants for
low-grade iron ore and CDW-grade barytes
Andhra Pradesh is India's top producer of
barytes
and accounts for nearly a quarter of world barytes production.
Andhra Pradesh is a leading producer of the listed minerals, has the stated leading position in mica, while Karnataka has the largest limestone reserves in the comparison.

secs.t: Mica belt - district, block mica, rank

x: Rajasthan is stated to rank second in the relevant comparison, while Andhra Pradesh’s position is not second.
Muscovite is white mica.
Rajasthan
has the Jaipur–Udaipur mica belt and ranks second in the stated comparison.

secs.t: Uranium and atomic minerals in beach sands

x: Thorium is obtained from
monazite and ilmenite beach sands
The National Geophysical Research Institute reported rare earth elements in
syenite rocks of Anantapur district
The current focus minerals specifically mentioned are
titanium, lithium and gallium
The initiative focuses on mapping critical minerals and promoting value addition through the Andhra Pradesh Mineral Development Corporation.

secs.t: Minor minerals and dimension stones → district

x: Black Galaxy is found in the Chimakurthy–Prakasam or Ongole belt, Srikakulam Blue in Srikakulam and Kashmir White or River White in Visakhapatnam.
Chilli Red is associated with Anantapur, Chocolate Brown with Kurnool, Vermiculite with Nellore and Chittoor, and Steatite with the Cuddapah system of Kadapa.
Building stone, gravel, clay and sand are minor minerals regulated by the States.

secs.t: Water resources of AP - basins, surface and groundwater, tanks

x: Godavari, Krishna and Pennar are the major basins, while Vamsadhara and Nagavali occur in the north.
Tanks are the traditional source of water in
Rayalaseema and the north coast
of Andhra Pradesh.

secs.t: Marine resources of AP - shelf, fishing harbours, salt pans

x: Andhra Pradesh plans port-based mineral beneficiation plants, linking mineral processing with the State’s coastal and port infrastructure.

secs.t: Forest resources of AP - MFP, red sanders, bamboo, GCC

x: Andhra Pradesh has 30,084.96 sq km of forest cover, which accounts for 23.59% of the State’s area.
Red sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) is endemic to the Seshachalam, Palakonda and Lankamalla hills of Rayalaseema.
GCC purchases products such as tamarind, honey, gum karaya and adda leaves.
The Girijan Cooperative Corporation is headquartered at
Visakhapatnam
and works with tribal communities in relation to minor forest produce.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Araku bauxite debate concerns mining versus tribal rights, along with wider ecological and forest-rights issues.
Swarnagiri gold mine was opened in Andhra Pradesh during June–July 2026, while the Meghalaya Assembly opposed uranium mining.
Bauxite mining in the Eastern Ghats raises ecological concerns and issues relating to PVTG rights under the Forest Conservation Act and Forest Rights Act.

rows.title: Climatic change and climatic regions - world, India and Andhra Pradesh

secs.t: Humid vs arid places - Thornthwaite moisture-based regions

x: The sequence is perhumid or wet, humid, semi-arid and arid.
The rain-shadow interior of the Deccan is semi-arid, not humid.
Thornthwaite’s classification considers precipitation effectiveness and
thermal efficiency
, with potential evapotranspiration serving as the basis for thermal efficiency.

secs.t: Trewartha regions of India - comparison with Koeppen

x: Trewartha modified Koeppen's temperature-rainfall approach and made it simpler for application to India.
Under Trewartha, Am denotes tropical rainforest in the west coast and North-East.
Trewartha's Caw corresponds broadly to Koeppen's
Cwg
for the Ganga plain, both indicating a humid subtropical or monsoonal climate with dry winter.

secs.t: Climatic regions of AP - Rayalaseema vs coastal belt

x: The deltaic region includes Konaseema, East and West Godavari and Krishna, and receives moderate rainfall mainly from the south-west monsoon.
The
Sileru and Sabari valleys
in the north coast receive the highest rainfall, about 140–152 cm.
The humid coast has high humidity and heavy rain; the deltaic region is fertile and river-fed; Rayalaseema is semi-arid; and the hills have cool micro-climates with local rain.

secs.t: Climate change signals in India - IMD trends, warming, extreme rainfall

x: 2024 was India's warmest year since 1901 and recorded 446 heatwave days, the highest number since 2000.
All three statements are correct: 2025 was about 1.43°C above pre-industrial levels, 2015-2025 were the eleven warmest years, and Himalayan heavy rainfall rose by about 50% since the 1950s.
The forecast of a below-normal 2026 monsoon for most of Andhra Pradesh cited
El Nino
as a contributing factor.

secs.t: Climate change impacts on AP - sea-level rise on deltas, heat waves, rainfall shift

x: The erosion at Uppada near Kakinada and along the Krishna coast is linked to rising seas and cyclonic waves.
The Godavari delta is sinking, and the rate of land subsidence exceeds the regional rise in sea level.
The projection indicates possible excess south-west monsoon rainfall in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu and warming above 1°C in around 40 coastal districts by 2040.

secs.t: Climate action plans - NAPCC missions and AP SAPCC

x: The eight NAPCC missions are Solar, Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture and Strategic Knowledge.
Adaptation spending was 5.6% of GDP in FY 2022, while SAPCCs moved from mitigation plans during 2010–15 to district-level, risk-based adaptation planning from 2020 onwards.
The APSES 2024–25 SAPCC report focused on
high-altitude tribal areas of the Eastern Ghats

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Climate types influence cropping decisions, and the Scarce Rainfall Zone requires lift-irrigation measures such as the Handri-Neeva type.
The stated AP climatic contrast includes Aw climate, the rain-shadow character of Rayalaseema and the cyclone-prone coast.
The relevant warning was the IMD’s
El Niño monsoon
warning.

units.title: Social Geography of the World, India and Andhra Pradesh - Distribution, Density, Growth, Sex Ratio, Literacy, Occupational Structure, SC/ST Population, Rural-Urban Components, Racial/Tribal/Religious/Linguistic Groups, Urbanisation, Migration and Metropolitan Regions

rows.title: World population - distribution, density, factors affecting distribution; population theories (Malthus)

secs.t: Population theories and writers - Malthus, neo-Malthusians, criticism

x: Exam angle: book-author pairs and "Malthusian theory relates to population".
Malthus argued that population tends to grow geometrically or exponentially, whereas food and resources increase only arithmetically.
Preventive checks reduce the birth rate and include moral restraint,
late marriage
and celibacy.
Technological progress, innovation and sustainable resource management have enabled resources and food production to grow faster than Malthus anticipated.

secs.t: Most populous countries - ranking, Muslim-majority, continents' shares

x: The ten most populous countries together account for about
60 percent
of the world's population.
India overtook China in
April 2023
, when India's population was approximately 1.4258 billion.
India's population was stated as 1.46 billion in 2025, while China's population peaked at 1.426 billion in 2022.
Brazil is the most populous country in South America.

secs.t: Density - densest and sparsest countries and continents

x: About 90 percent
of humanity lives on approximately 10 percent of the world's land area.
East Asia, including eastern China and Japan, and South Asia, including the Ganga plains and Bangladesh delta, are the two major dense population clusters.
The Ganges-Brahmaputra delta is among the most densely populated areas on Earth.

secs.t: Factors affecting distribution - physical vs socio-economic

x: The Sahara has a hot, dry desert climate that repels dense settlement; it is not an example of a moderate climate attracting population.
The north-eastern United States is a densely populated industrial-urban region and does not depend directly on agriculture in the manner of the Nile valley, Java or eastern China.

secs.t: UN observances and projections - World Population Day, WPP

x: The UN theme reported for 2026 was “
Realizing the hopes and aspirations of young people
.” Healthy Timing and Spacing of Pregnancies was India's MoHFW theme.
India's Ministry of Health and Family Welfare theme was
Healthy Timing and Spacing of Pregnancies
, abbreviated as HTSP.
The UNFPA State of World Population 2025 report was titled “
The Real Fertility Crisis
” and referred to a world population of 8.2 billion.

secs.t: Population milestones - billion marks and time taken

x: The population rose from 2 billion in 1927 to 3 billion in 1960, taking about 33 years, and from 7 billion in 2011 to 8 billion in 2022, taking about 11 years.
The milestones occurred in 1960, 1974, 1987 and 1999, giving intervals of 14, 13 and 12 years respectively.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Jakarta
is named as the largest city in the World Urbanisation Prospects 2025 reference.
India became the world’s most populous country in
April 2023
Fears associated with the Population Bomb influenced policy for decades, but the focus has increasingly shifted toward fertility decline.
The UNFPA Demographic Futures Survey was associated with the current-affairs reference dated
22 July 2026

rows.title: World population growth, demographic transition and regional patterns

secs.t: Rate of natural increase - from crude birth and death rates

x: Actual population growth equals natural increase, which is births minus deaths, plus
net migration
Positive growth occurs when births exceed deaths or when permanent net in-migration adds to the population.
The SRS 2024 values are CBR 18.3, CDR 6.4, IMR 24 and natural growth rate 11.9.
Counter-urbanisation denotes movement from urban to rural areas; place utility means destination desirability.

secs.t: Population milestones - billion marks and years between them

x: The population rose from five billion in 1987 to six billion in 1999, a period of 12 years.
The world population reached eight billion on
15 November 2022
The seven-billion mark was reached in 2011; the 1950 population was about 2.5 billion; and eight billion was more than three times that figure.

secs.t: World urbanisation patterns

x: Northern America, Latin America and Europe are among the most urbanised regions, whereas Africa and Asia are experiencing the fastest urban growth.
Jakarta, Dhaka, Tokyo and New Delhi are identified among the largest cities;
Cairo
is not included in that listed group.
Over-urbanisation occurs when urban population growth outpaces jobs and services, often resulting in slums.

secs.t: Ageing populations - ageing/shrinking countries, median age

x: Italy, Japan and South Korea
are noted for low birth rates, ageing populations and demographic decline.
Japan and Germany
are examples of Stage 5, characterised by very low birth rates, low death rates and declining population.
India's elderly population is projected to reach 325.3 million and the median age to rise to 40 years by 2051.

secs.t: Regional growth and projections - fastest regions, UN projections, sex ratio

x: Large inflows of male migrant workers produce highly male-skewed sex ratios in Gulf States.
The working-age shares were 85.7 per cent in the UAE and 85.6 per cent in Qatar, among the world's highest.
The WPP 2022 projected 8.5 billion people in 2030, 9.7 billion in 2050 and 10.4 billion in 2100.

secs.t: Dependency ratio - young vs old

x: A lower dependency ratio means that relatively fewer dependants are supported by the working-age population, creating
a potential demographic dividend
The Economic Survey 2025–26 cautions that a doubling of the dependency ratio will increase the importance of geriatric care as a growth-oriented employment sector.
Tamil Nadu’s old-age dependency ratio was 20.6 in 2021 and is projected to reach 32.7 by 2036.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The SRS 2024 TFR was cited as 1.9 and the NFHS-6 TFR as 2.0; both figures were discussed in the May–June 2026 context.
Andhra Pradesh is identified as being in DTM stage 4, with the policy emphasis shifting from population control to “Pillale Sampada”, meaning children are wealth.
The demographic dividend window is expected to close after 2041; therefore, skilling and creation of suitable jobs are time-bound priorities.

rows.title: India - population distribution and density; state-wise and district-wise patterns

secs.t: BIMARU states - term, coiner, profile

x: Their faster population growth is connected with the delimitation debate.
The BIMARU States are described as youthful States with high fertility and a wide window for demographic dividend.
BIMARU is formed from
Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh
The term BIMARU was coined by demographer
Ashish Bose
in the mid-1980s.

secs.t: State-wise population and area ranking

x: The correct order is Uttar Pradesh (16.49%), Maharashtra (9.29%), Bihar (8.58%) and undivided Andhra Pradesh (7.00%).
West Bengal ranked fourth with 7.55 per cent of India’s population, while undivided Andhra Pradesh ranked fifth with 7.00 per cent.
Residual Andhra Pradesh was placed 10th in population, with a 4.09 per cent share, and 8th in area, covering 1,62,970 square kilometres.

secs.t: Regions of high density - Ganga plains, deltas, mining-industrial districts

x: The
Ganga plain and the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta
are among the densely populated regions of the world.
The Godavari–Krishna coastal deltas have fertile alluvial and deltaic land and support intensive rice cultivation, favouring dense settlement.
Dhanbad’s high density is associated with coal mining, industrialisation and related employment.
Delhi had an urban share of 97.50 per cent and Chandigarh 97.25 per cent in the cited comparison.

secs.t: Factors of uneven distribution - plains, valleys, hills, deserts

x: Relief and water availability strongly influence the spatial concentration or dispersal of population.
Thin, rocky soils generally support sparse population because they constrain cultivation.
Although the Himalayas generally have sparse population, valleys such as Kashmir and parts of Himachal Pradesh have relatively higher density and are important exceptions.

secs.t: Population-resource regions of India

x: Progressive regions are resource-developed regions.

secs.t: Physiological and agricultural density

x: Physiological density measures total population in relation to net cultivated area.
All three formulae are correct.
Natality adds to population through natural increase, while immigration adds people from outside the region.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The
Registrar General of India
is retaining the existing Census Town criteria for Census 2027, although the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs described them as outdated before a parliamentary panel.
Administrative boundaries may include non-built-up rural land or exclude functionally connected built-up areas, causing peri-urban areas to be misclassified.

rows.title: India - population growth: decadal trends, growth rate, Census 2011 highlights
sub: Group-II S2-50: Demographics of India - population size, growth, distribution and density

secs.t: India's share of world population vs share of world area

x: India:
2.4% of world surface area
(3.278 million sq km) but
17.7% of world population
Older answers:
and "about
" of the world - these reflect earlier data.
India's 2011 population about equalled USA + Indonesia + Brazil + Pakistan + Bangladesh + Japan combined.

secs.t: Census 2011 highlights - population, decadal growth, growth rate, child population

x: Census 2011 recorded 62.33 crore males, 58.76 crore females and a rural share of 68.9 per cent.
The urban population constituted
31.1 per cent
of India's population in Census 2011, amounting to about 37.71 crore persons.
The growth rate declined from 21.54 per cent in 1991–2001 to 17.7 per cent in 2001–2011, a fall of about 3.9 percentage points.
The 0–6 child population was 1,644.15 lakh, about 13.6 per cent of the total, and was the first absolute fall in decades.
Andhra Pradesh accounted for about
4.09 per cent
of India's population in 2011; some tabulations round it to 4.10 per cent.

secs.t: State-wise growth - highest, lowest, negative

x: Dadra and Nagar Haveli
recorded the highest decadal growth among Union Territories, at about 55.9 per cent.
Andhra Pradesh recorded a decadal growth rate of
9.21 per cent
during 2001–2011, below the national rate of 17.7 per cent.
Andhra Pradesh recorded its peak decadal growth of 21.13 per cent during

secs.t: Age structure - elderly and children

x: The 15–59 age group constituted 66.4 per cent, larger than the 0–14 group at 24 per cent and the 60-plus group at 9.7 per cent.
About
130 million
Indians were estimated to be aged 65 years and above in 2026.
The 60-plus population is projected to increase from about 100 million in 2011 to
230 million
by 2036, or about one in seven Indians.

secs.t: Decadal trends - phases of growth and the year of great divide

x: After 1981, later marriage and female education contributed to a fall in the crude birth rate, producing a high-but-declining growth phase.
The chronological order is 1951, 1971, 2001 and 2011; their recorded growth figures were 13.31, 24.80, 21.54 and 17.64 percent respectively.
The peak decadal growth rate was 24.80 percent during
, often described as the explosion decade in the relevant classification.
The annual compound growth rate rose from about 0.19 percent during 1891–1921 to approximately
2.15 percent
in the later period.

secs.t: Census history - first census, first synchronous census, number

x: The 1872 census was non-synchronous, whereas the 1881 census was the first complete and synchronous census and was conducted under Lord Ripon.
Regular decennial census operations began with the first complete and synchronous census of 1881.
The census is conducted under the Census Act, 1948, and census matters fall under Union List Entry 69 within the constitutional framework of Article 246.

secs.t: Upcoming Census - caste enumeration and digital census

x: Digital literacy
, along with bank accounts, is cited as an example of a new subject in Census 2027.
House Listing and Housing Census is planned for April–September 2026, followed by Population Enumeration in February 2027, with 1 March 2027 as the reference date.
Population Enumeration was advanced in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Uttarakhand and Goa, while it was deferred in Manipur.
The 84th Amendment is linked to the delimitation freeze, while the 106th Amendment and Article 334A are linked to the framework for women's reservation.

A Census Town is a village-status settlement meeting all three criteria: population of at least 5,000, at least 75 percent of male workers outside agriculture, and density of at least 400 persons per square kilometre.

The Registrar General of India is expected to retain the Census Town category for Census 2027, although the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs considers it outdated because of male bias and uniform thresholds.

secs.t: Population density - definition, trend, highest/lowest states and UTs, South India, AP

x: Exam angle: "lowest density among Odisha / Assam / Jharkhand / Arunachal" → Arunachal Pradesh.
All four pairs are correct for the 2011 figures given: Delhi 11,320, Chandigarh 9,258, Puducherry 2,598 and Andaman and Nicobar Islands 46 persons per square kilometre.
On the 28-district map, Visakhapatnam had the highest density at 1,870 persons per square kilometre, while Polavaram had the lowest at 54.
Bihar recorded 1,106 persons per square kilometre, West Bengal 1,028, Kerala 860 and Arunachal Pradesh 17.
The ascending order is Arunachal Pradesh (17), Andaman and Nicobar Islands (46), Mizoram (52) and Sikkim (86).

secs.t: Distribution of population - most/least populous states, BIMARU

x: The listed least populous units are Lakshadweep, Daman and Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Sikkim and Chandigarh, in that order.
Population
growth was faster in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan than in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh

secs.t: Population projections - India overtaking China, UN WPP

x: UN WPP 2024 places India’s share of the world population at approximately
17.7 percent
India’s estimated population was 1,363.0 million in 2021 and is projected to reach 1,522.3 million by 2036.
The projection of 1,522.3 million by 2036 was prepared by the Technical Group on Population Projections under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Southern States, including Andhra Pradesh, fear a reduction in their seat share because delimitation based on population may disadvantage States that controlled population growth.
Former officials have expressed concern that details of parents may create possible links between the National Population Register and the National Register of Citizens.
The Registrar General of India is retaining the Census Town definition formulated in 1981.

rows.title: Demographic dividend, ageing and population policy
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I D-59

secs.t: Demographic dividend - definition, working-age group, India's window, policies

x: Exam angle: the age group (15-64) and the "rise in share of working people" definition are the most-asked points.
The UNFPA estimate identifies
as the world's longest demographic dividend window.
UN projections cited in the Economic Survey 2025–26 place the peak share of the 15–59 working-age population at about
65 percent
around 2030.
Demographic dividend can operate through greater labour supply, higher savings and investment, a lower dependency ratio and the release of human capital.
Andhra Pradesh combines a 9.21% growth rate with a large youth workforce, but its literacy rate of 67.35% lags, requiring a shift towards learning outcomes and skills.

secs.t: Population theories and authors

x: Exam angle: UPPSC 2024 asked the Malthusian blanks (geometric, arithmetic).
Warren Thompson propounded demographic transition theory in 1929, Edwin Cannan propounded optimum population theory, and Frank Notestein formalised demographic transition theory.
The Marxian view does not regard overpopulation as a purely natural phenomenon; it considers it a product of capitalism, associated with relative surplus population and unemployment.

Warren Thompson is associated with demographic transition theory, Frank Notestein with its formal three-stage formulation, Edwin Cannan with optimum population, and Paul Ehrlich with The Population Bomb.

secs.t: Demographic history - British period, literacy and mortality at independence

x: The British period was marked by high birth and death rates, frequent famines and epidemics, and generally poor demographic conditions.
In 1951, overall literacy was 18.33%, with male literacy at 27.2% and female literacy at 8.9%.
Life expectancy in India around 1951 was approximately
32 years
Population-control efforts were continued during the Sixth, Seventh and Eighth Plans.

secs.t: Ageing and dependency - elderly share, dependency ratio, median age, LASI

x: The population aged 60 years and above is projected to reach about
347 million
by 2050, constituting nearly one-fifth of the population.
The estimated reduction in annual GDP growth due to ageing is
70 basis points
All four statements are correct: Kerala and Tamil Nadu are ageing fastest, 18.7% of elderly women live alone, 78% lack pension cover and 70% depend on others.
The SRS 2024 total fertility rate is 1.9, and the RBI refers to Kerala and Tamil Nadu as ageing States by 2036; no zero dependency ratio is stated.

secs.t: Total Fertility Rate - replacement level, NFHS-5, states, population bills

x: Total fertility rate is the average number of children per woman over the reproductive age span of
15–49 years
Among the identified values,
Meghalaya
had a TFR of 2.9, higher than Bihar at 3.0 only if Bihar is included; the stated NFHS-5 list records Bihar at 3.0.
Andhra Pradesh has a TFR of
; the fall was described by the State Health Minister as alarming and linked to the expression ‘shrinconomics’.
The February 2026 policy shifts the emphasis from population control to managing ageing and deriving benefits from the demographic dividend.
NFHS-6 reported the
Andaman and Nicobar Islands
as having India’s lowest TFR.

secs.t: Family planning - FIRST programme, methods, Emergency, Mission Parivar Vikas

x: Coercive mass sterilisation was associated with the Emergency period of
, followed by the 1976 policy.
Female sterilisation was the dominant method and was reported for
of married women in NFHS-5, compared with 36% in NFHS-4.
ASHAs counsel a two-year gap after marriage before the first child and a three-year interval between births.
Mission Parivar Vikas provided for Clinical Outreach Teams in 146 districts.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Southern States that reduced fertility face concerns about
lower tax devolution and fewer seats after delimitation
China, Japan and South Korea
are cited as countries that grew rapidly during their demographic-dividend phase.
Both statements are true, and the combination of low fertility and a relatively high median age explains why Andhra Pradesh is ageing faster than India.

rows.title: India - sex ratio and child sex ratio: trends, regional pattern, causes
sub: Group-II S2-51: Sex ratio and child sex ratio - India and Andhra Pradesh

secs.t: Sex ratio of states and UTs - Census 2011 values

x: Exam angle: match-the-state-with-value questions; memorise the four values above plus Kerala and Haryana.
Puducherry recorded 1,037, Tamil Nadu 996, Lakshadweep 946 and undivided Andhra Pradesh 993 females per 1,000 males in 2011.
In 2001, Kerala recorded 1,058, Haryana 861, Puducherry 1,001 and Daman and Diu 710 females per 1,000 males.
The Andhra Pradesh sex ratio was 981 in 1971, 978 in 1981, 976 in 1991, 983 in 2001 and 997 in 2011.
Polavaram had the highest sex ratio at 1,051, while Markapuram had the lowest at 962 among the 28 districts considered.
Polavaram
recorded the highest sex ratio in the 28-district map, with 1,051 females per 1,000 males.

secs.t: Missing women - coiner and meaning

x: Nobel laureate
Amartya Sen
introduced the concept of ‘missing women’ in 1990 to describe the demographic deficit of women, particularly in Asia.
‘Missing women’ denotes the demographic deficit of women resulting from intra-household discrimination, neglect of female health and sex-selective abortion.

secs.t: Sex ratio definition - Indian vs international convention

x: Child sex ratio
is the number of girls per 1,000 boys in the 0–6 years age group.
SRB measures
girls born per 1,000 boys born
The sex ratio was lowest in 1991 at 927 females per 1,000 males.
The sex ratios were 946 in 1951, 941 in 1961, 930 in 1971 and 934 in 1981.

secs.t: Causes of adverse sex ratio

x: High maternal mortality, high female child mortality and female foeticide are accepted causes of an adverse sex ratio.
Son preference and patriarchal norms sustain gender bias, which has been described as deep-seated even though conditions have improved.
The study reported that heat exposure during pregnancy is linked to
fewer male births

secs.t: Sex ratio at birth vs overall sex ratio - SRS, CRS, NFHS

x: Arunachal Pradesh
recorded the best sex ratio at birth under CRS 2024, at 1,050; Kerala recorded 970.
British-period conditions were marked by overall literacy below 16%, female literacy around 7%, infant mortality around 218 per 1,000 and life expectancy around 32 years.
The biological norm is about
105 boys per 100 girls
, equivalent to roughly 950 girls per 1,000 boys at birth.
All three statements describe the normal biological pattern: more boys are born, male child mortality is naturally higher, and the corresponding ratio is about 950 girls per 1,000 boys.
India’s child sex ratio was 927 in 2001; the 2011 figure was reported as 918 or 919 depending on the source, while 914 was the provisional figure.

secs.t: Child sex ratio (0-6) - trend and lowest states

x: The child sex ratio declined from 976 in 1961 to 927 in 2001 and to the reported 2011 figures of 914 provisionally or 919 in the India Year Book.
The cited 2011 child sex ratios were 834 for Haryana and 846 for Punjab, while Mizoram and Meghalaya were the best-performing States at about 970.

secs.t: Trends since 1901 - rising and falling phases

x: The figures correspond successively to 1901 (972), 1941 (945), 1991 (927) and 2011 (943).
The low point of 927 was recorded in 1991, after which the ratio rose to 933 in 2001 and 943 in 2011.
The Andhra Pradesh figures were 978 in 1981, 976 in 1991, 983 in 2001 and 997 in 2011; the decline until 1991 was followed by improvement.

secs.t: Schemes and laws - BBBP, PCPNDT Act

x: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao was launched in 2015 to
reverse the declining child sex ratio
through multi-sectoral action.
Son preference, female foeticide, neglect of girls, maternal mortality and male-selective migration are identified causes; equal treatment of girls is not a cause of adverse sex-ratio trends.
The Supreme Court observed that the child sex ratio showed clear signs of improvement, but sex selection continued to reflect
deep-seated patriarchy

secs.t: Sex ratio across religions and social groups (SC, ST)

x: All three statements are correct: the Indian ST sex ratio was 990, the overall figure was reported as 940/943, and the Andhra Pradesh ST sex ratio was 1,009.
Christians
had the highest sex ratio among the listed religious communities, at 1,023.
The sex ratio of Scheduled Castes was 945 according to the stated Census 2011 comparison.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Andhra Pradesh is cited at 997 for sex ratio and 944 for child sex ratio, compared with India’s 943 and 918 respectively; both State values are higher.
NFHS-5 was the first NFHS in which the estimated number of women exceeded the number of men, reflected in its sex ratio of 1,020.

rows.title: India - literacy: levels, gender and regional gaps, trends
sub: Group-II S2-52: Literacy and educational attainment - India and Andhra Pradesh

secs.t: Literacy campaigns and missions - TLC first district, Saakshar Bharat, New India Literacy Programme, NEP 2020

x: Exam angle: "first" facts (district, UT, state) and scheme age group (15+).
The correct sequence is Farmers' Functional Literacy Programme (1967-68), National Adult Education Programme (1978), National Literacy Mission (1988), and Saakshar Bharat (2009).
The five components are
Foundational Literacy and Numeracy, Critical Life Skills, Basic Education, Vocational Skills and Continuing Education
Andhra Pradesh implemented ULLAS across all 26 districts, with 41,500 SHG volunteer teachers serving 4,15,000 learners from classes beginning on 5 November 2024.
The identified focus groups include SHG members, school cooks, helpers, night watchmen and anganwadi ayahs.

The Community Development Programme began in 1952, the National Extension Service in 1953, the National Adult Education Programme in 1978, and the Integrated Rural Development Programme began in 1978–79 before its nationwide expansion in 1980.

secs.t: Literacy Census 2011 - definition of literate (age threshold), national rate, male vs female

x: A literate person is aged seven years or above and must be able to both read and write with understanding in any language.
The final Census 2011 literacy rate was
, or 72.98% when expressed more precisely.
AP recorded 67.35%, 74.77% and 59.96% for total, male and female literacy, respectively, compared with India’s 72.98%, 80.88% and 64.63%.
Visakhapatnam had the highest literacy at 79.05 per cent, Alluri Sitarama Raju the lowest at 44.67 per cent, Polavaram the highest sex ratio and Markapuram the lowest.

secs.t: State ranking - highest/lowest literacy states and UTs

x: PLFS 2023-24 reported an overall literacy rate of
for persons aged seven years and above.
The PLFS-based top units were Mizoram, Lakshadweep and Nagaland, while Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and Madhya Pradesh were at the bottom of the cited grouping.
The AP literacy rate was 69.10% in PLFS 2018-19, 72.60% in PLFS 2023-24 and 71.40% for calendar year 2025 as cited.

secs.t: Gender gap in literacy - largest-gap states

x: Rajasthan
had the largest gender gap in literacy, at 28 percentage points.
The national gender gap in literacy in 2011 was about
16 percentage points
The cited causes include distance to schools and safety, early marriage, dowry, son preference and poverty.
PLFS 2023-24 recorded male literacy of 87.2% and female literacy of 74.6%.

secs.t: Rural-urban literacy differential

x: The Census 2011 provisional rural literacy rate was 68.9%, while the urban rate was 85.0%.
PLFS 2023-24 reported urban literacy of 88.9% and rural literacy of 77.5%, leaving a gap of about 11 percentage points.
Rural women
face the largest literacy deficit.

secs.t: Trends since 1951 - decadal improvement

x: The literacy rates rose from 18.33% in 1951 to 28.30% in 1961, 43.57% in 1981 and 64.83% in 2001.
The largest decadal gain came in the 1990s, culminating in the 1991 Census period.
The Andhra Pradesh sequence was 29.94% in 1981, 45.86% in 1991, 62.07% in 2001 and 67.35% in 2011.

secs.t: Literacy among SC/ST populations

x: The cited 2011 literacy rate was 66.1% for Scheduled Castes and 59.0% for Scheduled Tribes.
The cited figures were 48.8% for Scheduled Tribe literacy in Andhra Pradesh and 49.5% in Telangana.
Low literacy is one of the four criteria used in relation to
Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups
(PVTGs).
Scheduled Caste literacy was reported at about 66.1%, lower than the national average of approximately 73–74%.

secs.t: District-wise literacy of AP - most and least literate

x: Visakhapatnam
recorded the highest literacy rate among the 28 districts, at 79.05%.
Alluri Sitarama Raju had the lowest literacy rate among the 28 districts, at
In the 13-district era,
West Godavari
had the highest literacy rate, at 74.6%.
Vizianagaram recorded the lowest literacy rate in the 13-district era, at 58.9%.

secs.t: Education policy and schemes - NEP 2020, Operation Blackboard, Samagra Shiksha, Nadu-Nedu

x: Operation Blackboard provided basic facilities such as two rooms, two teachers and teaching aids.
Samagra Shiksha is an umbrella scheme covering education from
pre-school to Class 12
Samagra Shiksha was launched in 2018 and subsumed Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan and Teacher Education.
NEP 2020 targets 50% gross enrolment ratio in higher education by 2035 and 100% GER from pre-school to secondary level by 2030.

secs.t: Educational attainment - FLN Index, GER, dropout, UDISE+, AISHE

x: Punjab
recorded the highest FLN score in the second edition of the FLN Index.
Female GER in higher education increased from 28.5 to 30.2 during 2021–23, with the later figure representing 2022–23.
All three statements are correct: female higher-education GER reached 30.2, exceeded male GER, and gender parity was reported at all school levels.

secs.t: 100 percent literacy villages and hamlets in AP

x: Under ULLAS, the national benchmark for being fully literate is 95% literacy among persons aged 15 years and above.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The chronological order is Census 2011, PLFS 2018–19, PLFS 2025 and PLFS 2023–24 only if the dates are treated strictly by year; however, among the listed reporting periods, the intended sequence is
A, B, D, C
based on the stated year labels.
Census and PLFS use different samples and methodologies; the PLFS rate cited here uses the same 7+ definition, so the figures are not directly comparable merely as equivalent estimates.

rows.title: India - occupational structure: main and marginal workers, work participation rate, cultivators and agricultural labourers
sub: Group-II S2-53: Occupational structure and work participation - India and Andhra Pradesh

secs.t: Census worker categories - main vs marginal workers; cultivators, agricultural labourers, household industry, other workers - shares

x: The Census Town criteria are population of 5,000 or more, 75 per cent or more of male main workers in non-agricultural activities, and population density of at least 400 persons per sq km.
The Census Town criteria remained unchanged since 1981 and were retained for
Census 2027
Cultivators numbered 1,188.08 lakh, agricultural labourers 1,443.34 lakh, household industry workers 183.38 lakh, and other workers 2,004.09 lakh.
Agricultural labourers
had 581.65 lakh marginal workers, higher than cultivators, household industry workers and other workers.
Agricultural labourers constituted the largest component of Andhra Pradesh’s main workforce, numbering
86.12 lakh
, or about 45% of its main workers.

secs.t: Work participation rate - male vs female, rural vs urban, state variations

x: Both statements are true, and the greater need for manual labour in subsistence-based activities explains the relatively higher WPR in these regions.
Dividing 230.81 lakh workers by 495.77 lakh population gives an approximate WPR of
, higher than the all-India rate.
Work participation is higher in several less developed areas because subsistence needs lead to greater reliance on manual labour.

secs.t: Sectoral distribution of workforce - primary, secondary, tertiary shares

x: Agriculture’s share of workers declined from 58.2% in 2001 to 54.6% in 2011, while the secondary and tertiary shares increased.
For July–September 2025, agriculture accounted for 42.4% of total employment, self-employment 55.8%, and casual labour 18.9%.
The rural agricultural share fell from 58.5% to 55.8%; rural secondary and tertiary shares were 22.6% and 21.7%, respectively.

secs.t: Cultivators vs agricultural labourers - trend of shift

x: Andhra Pradesh had 110.52 lakh agricultural labourers, comprising 86.12 lakh main and 24.40 lakh marginal workers, and they formed about 48% of its workers.
Men’s out-migration
has increased women’s participation in farm work, even though women hold only 12.8% of operational holdings.
The agrarian hierarchy broadly corresponds with the caste hierarchy: upper castes have historically owned more land, while Scheduled Castes are largely marginal farmers and landless labourers.

secs.t: PLFS indicators - LFPR, WPR, unemployment rate definitions

x: Exam angle: WPR's denominator is total population; LFPR's includes the unemployed.
Under UPSS, a person is considered employed if he or she worked for at least 30 days in the year.
The January–March 2026 CWS figures were
LFPR 55.5 per cent, female LFPR 34.7 per cent and WPR 52.8 per cent
The youth unemployment rate for persons aged 15–29 was
9.9 per cent
in annual PLFS 2025.
Headline PLFS rates are generally reported for
persons aged 15 years and above
, unless the question specifies another age range.

secs.t: Female work participation - levels and regional contrast

x: Female LFPR rose from 23.3% in 2017–18 to 30% in 2019–20, 37% in 2022–23 and about 40% in 2025.
Universal availability of flexible working hours
was not identified as a reason for the rise.
Mechanisation, greater participation of girls in education, lack of flexible hours, workplace distance, safety concerns and family duties have contributed to low female work participation.

secs.t: Non-workers categories and dependency

x: There were 7,288.27 lakh non-workers in 2011, amounting to about 60% of the population.
The Census categories include students, household-duty persons, dependants, pensioners, rentiers, beggars or vagrants and others.
The working-age group aged 15–59 rose to 66.4% of the population, while the 0–14 age group declined to 24%.

secs.t: AP district-wise occupational data - cultivators and agricultural labourers

x: West Godavari
had the highest share of agricultural labourers among total workers in 2011, associated with its delta paddy economy.

secs.t: Employment programmes - MGNREGA, PMEGP

x: PMEGP was launched in 2008 by merging the Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana and the Rural Employment Generation Programme.
PMEGP is under the Ministry of MSME, KVIC acts as the nodal agency, and the programme provides credit-linked subsidy for micro-enterprises.
NAPS concerns apprenticeships, whereas credit-linked subsidy for micro-enterprises is a feature of PMEGP.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The one-hour CWS criterion can classify a person as employed even when work is insufficient, thereby hiding underemployment.
A lower unemployment rate may reflect
distress entry into low-productivity work
rather than the creation of decent or secure employment.
The one-hour CWS rule, rising unpaid family work and distress entry into low-productivity work may conceal distress and underemployment.

rows.title: India - Scheduled Caste population: distribution and concentration

secs.t: States/UTs with no notified SC population - list and reasons

x: Scheduled Castes were notified in 31 States and Union Territories, covering 1,241 groups.
The populations concerned are overwhelmingly tribal.
The 83rd Amendment of 2000 removed the need for Scheduled Caste reservation in Arunachal Pradesh panchayats because the State is wholly tribal.
Scheduled Caste status is available to Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists.

secs.t: States with highest SC share vs highest absolute SC population

x: Punjab
had the highest Scheduled Caste share at about 31.9%, followed by Himachal Pradesh at 25.2% and West Bengal at 23.5%.
Mizoram had the lowest Scheduled Caste share among States with Scheduled Castes, at about 0.1%.
Andhra Pradesh had about 84.69 lakh Scheduled Castes, constituting approximately
of India’s Scheduled Caste population.

secs.t: SC population Census 2011 - national share and count

x: The Scheduled Caste population included about 1,035.35 lakh males and 978.43 lakh females, giving an approximate sex ratio of 945 females per 1,000 males.
The Scheduled Caste population of Andhra Pradesh rose from 32.73 lakh in 1971 to
84.69 lakh
The Scheduled Caste population of India was
20.14 crore
, or 201.4 million, according to Census 2011 data.

secs.t: District-level concentration - highest SC share districts

x: Koch Bihar
district of West Bengal recorded the highest Scheduled Caste share, at about 50%.
Shahid Bhagat Singh Nagar had a Scheduled Caste share above 40%, not about 20%.
Scheduled Castes are relatively dense in fertile alluvial plains such as Punjab, the Ganga plain, West Bengal and coastal deltas, where settled farming historically used landless labour.

secs.t: Rural-urban distribution of SCs

x: In 2011, approximately 76% of Scheduled Castes lived in rural areas and 24% in urban areas; their shares were about 18.5% of the rural population and 12.6% of the urban population.
Scheduled Tribes are even more rural than Scheduled Castes; about 89.97% of the ST population lived in rural areas.

secs.t: Literacy and occupational profile of SCs vs national average

x: Scheduled Caste unemployment was 5.5% against 5% nationally, while SC infant mortality was 44 against 32.
The enrolment shares were OBC 49%, General 27%, Scheduled Caste 17% and Scheduled Tribe 10%, giving the order
A, C, D, B
Punjab
was noted as having one of the highest Scheduled Caste enrolment shares.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Census 2027 is described as the first enumeration of all castes in independent India, rather than an enumeration limited to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
A post-2026 delimitation may re-fix Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe reserved seats according to new Census shares, creating a fear of seat loss among southern States.
